speakeroldname: Hon. Richard A. Bell (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: MODIFICATION OF PROCEDURES RESPECTING ILLEGAL CHINESE ENTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise the house of certain far reaching modifications in procedures relating to the investigation into illegal Chinese immigration, which has been under way since early 1960.
First, as a result of the convictions registered against a score or more of illegal immigration agents and the confessions of several hundred Chinese immigrants that they entered Canada illegally, it is believed that substantial
success has been attained in exposing and breaking up the illegal Chinese immigration system and in drastically reducing the number of attempted fraudulent entries to Canada. Since the principal objectives of the investigation have now been largely achieved, the house will be pleased to learn that so far as the massive large scale investigation of thousands of Chinese already in Canada is concerned, we consider that we have reached the point where this can now be brought to a close. Prosecutions before the courts and those already recommended will naturally proceed to completion.
Hon. members know that Canadians of Chinese descent generally are amongst our most law abiding citizens and therefore will welcome the termination of this massive investigation.
Second, the Hong Kong policemen at present in Canada will be returned to Hong Kong in the very near future.
Third, new and greatly simplified procedures are being adopted for adjusting the status of those Chinese already in Canada who may still desire to come forward and make a voluntary statement as to their illegal status in this country. The essence of this new procedure will be the elimination generally of collateral interviews and the taking of a simple statement under oath after interview with the person principally concerned, correcting the false record previously given as to his true identity and family relationships. This interview will be carried out in the presence of the person's legal adviser, if requested, and the new and correct information about the individual's true identity will be embodied in a statutory declaration under the Canada Evidence Act.
I must emphasize that further false statements would be detrimental to the individual. Where it is established that in this interview and statement false information has once again been given, the individual will have perjured himself and will thereafter be debarred from sponsoring applications for relatives or other intending immigrants to Canada. My officials and I will deal sympathetically and honourably with all Chinese immigrants who will deal truthfully and honourably with us. We would like to have all those who entered Canada illegally prior to 1960 take advantage of this simple procedure to adjust their personal status, but no pressures will be brought to bear. It is a matter

Immigration Modifications of personal choice, but it must be evident that the course of wisdom for everyone would be to adjust his status on a truthful basis.
Fourth, a program to expedite greatly the processing of applications by Chinese immigrants for Canadian citizenship has been adopted.
With these new arrangements in effect, placing the emphasis on a simplified adjustment procedure, a sworn statement under oath and sanctions against those who attempt hereafter to falsify the evidence, I am confident that we will be able to maintain in the future the control which we have succeeded, as a result of the efforts of the past three years, in establishing over illegal and fraudulent applications. With the full co-operation of the members of the Chinese community across Canada, I am hopeful that we can turn the page to a new phase of the immigration story.

speechtext:
Since you have mentioned my name, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief comment in the hope that even if your ruling is already prepared it will take into consideration the point I wish to make.
It seems to me that the main point of the complaint which was made on November 1 by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was perhaps missed, namely that there was one question in the set of questions passed as an order for return to which there was no answer at all.
I recognize that members have no right to require this or that kind of answer from a minister. I recognize that on orders of the day, when verbal questions are put such as are sometimes asked of ministers, the minister can sit still. However, when a question has been passed by the house as an order, it seems to me that the government is required to give some kind of answer. In this particular instance there was a question which read, "If not, why not?" To that question there was no answer at all. The government in giving an answer might say, "Not applicable" or "Not in the public interest" or it might give any one of a number of answers. However, to give no answer at all is, I submit, not complying with the order of the house.
I stress the point which was made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, that before such a question is passed as an order for return the minister has an opportunity to scrutinize the question and make it an order for return, except for this part or that part. However, when that is not done; when the minister agrees that a question should be passed as an order for return, that becomes an order of the house, and I submit that an answer of some sort should be given to all parts of the question. As I say, in this particular question there was that part which read "If not, why not?", to which there was no answer at all. I think that is the point at issue.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ANSWER TO ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words about this matter in elaboration of the matter I raised as a point of privilege, as Your Honour pointed out. It is that the true essence of this matter has to be considered,
Statement by Mr. Speaker and when a minister says, "Order for return" in response to a question, what he is doing in shorthand form is making a motion. Otherwise, there could not be an order of the house, as Your Honour would recognize at once. There cannot be an order of the house unless the house has made a decision. The only way in which the house can make a decision is to have a proposition put before it. We have acquiesced in this brief way of doing this, and that is the essence of the matter.
At any time when a minister seeks to make a question an order for return it would, of course, be competent for a member to ask Your Honour to call the yeas and nays. This demonstrates quite clearly that what is being done at that time is to make an order of the house. I think Your Honour's predecessor made a decision on that point in the last parliament, that it is competent to ask for the yeas and nays when a minister proposes that a question be made an order for return. If that point has not been drawn to Your Honour's attention I will not give the reference now, because I know we do not want to have a lengthy discussion at this stage, but I suggest that aspect of the matter be further considered. But once the house has accepted the minister's suggestion, which is in fact a motion, that a question be made an order for return, then the house has ordered the ministry to comply with it in the precise language in which it is phrased, unless the minister in asking for it to be an order for return, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, makes some reservation and asks that it be changed in some fashion, which is quite often done, particularly with motions for papers.
My point is that while the ministers are perfectly free to give whatever kind of answers they choose to the questions of an individual hon. member, and as Your Honour has often pointed out quite correctly we have no recourse except to make it a grievance at some particular time, once an order of the house is made the government, being the servant of the house, is responsible for carrying out that order precisely in the terms in which it is made.
That is my whole point, and I speak with some assurance on this point because some years ago when I held the office now held by the hon. member for London (Mr. Hal-penny), I was told by the prime minister of that day that it was my duty to scrutinize all these questions and make sure no question was made an order for return which would ask for anything which the government would not wish to produce, and that proper

Statement by Mr. Speaker objection should be taken at the proper time before an order of the house was made. I submit that if the Minister of Veterans Affairs, in the particular matter that was before the house, felt that it was not a proper question to have been made an order of the house he should have taken exception to it, or he should have answered the question in the house itself and then the whole problem would not have arisen.
As Your Honour knows, a minister can be called to the bar of the house for his failure to comply with an order of the house, and it seems to me there is a fundamental question involved of the rights of parliament.

The rule, which is 39 (4), reads as follows:
If a question is of such a nature that, in the opinion of the minister who is to furnish the reply, such reply should be in the form of a return, and the minister states that he has no objection to laying such return upon the table of the house, his statement shall, unless otherwise ordered by the house, be deemed an order of the house to that effect-
An order of the house was accordingly made that I should give a reply in the form of a return. In the form of a return simply means that it is not an oral answer but a typed or printed answer which is placed on the table and is then recorded in the records of the house. Giving it in the form of a return I assumed that I was operating under the same rules that apply when answers are required to oral questions, that if the question cannot be answered in the form in which it is written, then no answer is required from the minister.
In this particular instance I examined to see whether or not I could produce an answer to the "If not, why not?" question, at that time assuming that this was a proper question-I now know that it is not-and I was unable to find in the records any conclusion with regard to that particular part of the question. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ANSWER TO ORDER FOR RETURN
speechtext:
I have listened to the observations of hon. gentlemen in this regard. First of all I would preface my remarks by indicating that standing order 39(4) does apply.

Statement by Mr. Speaker I would particularly underline a point which I think has been missed both by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Standing order 39(4) says:
If a question is of such a nature that, in the opinion of the minister who is to furnish the reply, such reply should be in the form of a return,-
This is the point which I think hon. members have missed, that it shall be "in the form of a return".
-and the minister states that he has no objection to laying such return upon the table of the house his statement shall, unless otherwise ordered by the house-
This refers to the point made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
-be deemed an order of the house to that effect-
The "effect" is that it shall be made in the form of a return.
-and the same shall be entered in the Votes and Proceedings as such
In other words, the order of the house is that the minister's answer shall be in the form of a return. It is not the order that the question shall be answered as it appears; it is merely to supply the information in the form of a return. We know that when a motion is before the house for the production of papers in the form of a return, there is nothing which indicates the precise nature of what shall be included. In the same way, when a minister, replying to a written or a starred question, says "Order for return tabled herewith", there is nothing there which says that every portion of that question has been answered.
I fully appreciate that the hon. member has said that this is a short method of putting a motion and dealing with it.
I would refer hon. members to Bourinot, page 244 of his fourth edition, under the title "Presentation of Papers", where he states:
Questions put by members are sometimes made equivalent to a motion for papers under rule 37.
That is now standing order 39. Now we get to the matter of whether an answer should be given to every portion of a question. I face immediately the problem of who is to judge the sufficiency of the answer. It is not open to hon. members to do so. It is not open to the Chair to determine whether such an answer is sufficient. And regardless of what might have been the particular parts of the question, the answer could be made the most capricious of answers one could imagine. To use the example of "If not, why not?", the minister could make the most capricious reply which I think could be devised and simply say "Because", and who would be able to judge the sufficiency of such reply?


Therefore I think we are belabouring the point here. I can see nothing further or different in this particular instance from an order for return tabled herewith, or than any other written question answered by a minister. As I indicated the other day, I felt there had been a suggestion of setting up a double standard in dealing with questions, and that I could not accept because to me there is no one who can judge the sufficiency of the answer.
In so far as whether there has been a defiance or an improper reply, I think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and others have indicated, as has been done by my predecessors, that a grossly or obviously improper answer might found a grievance. There are times when grievances can be aired, and I think that is when such a matter as has been under discussion could be raised. I do not think this is a matter of privilege; I think it is a matter of grievance. In my estimation there is no such thing as an order that the paragraph of a question shall be answered seriatim; the order is in the form of a return. That would be my ruling on that point.
In so far as the matter of "If not, why not?" and other such questions are concerned, I would suggest that we defer that to some day next week, because hon. members may wish to prepare for it. I am prepared to raise the matter and deal with it, because I have noticed that on the order paper there are presently two or three questions which I think, with all due respect, are not proper questions, as they raise certain points of order. Therefore I would prefer to have hon. members prepare themselves so that we can have a discussion.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister. Having regard to recent developments in the bay of Fundy, and having regard to the information we received yesterday that no progress has been made internationally in agreement on a wider zone of territorial and jurisdictional waters, is the government now prepared to establish immediately by national action a six mile territorial zone and a six mile jurisdictional and fisheries zone in addition, which it has been unable to secure by international action, reserving of course specific historic rights in the larger zone?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ANSWER TO ORDER FOR RETURN
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EXTENSION OF TERRITORIAL WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman knows, over a period of years when he held the position of secretary of state for external affairs this was a matter which received consideration, but at no time during the period in which he or his predecessor, Mr. St. Laurent, occupied the position was there ever any suggestion that by unilateral
Inquiries of the Ministry action the government of Canada could proceed in a manner that would not place Canadian fishermen in a very difficult position in relation to the United States in the markets that Canadian fishermen have in that country.
This question of the establishment of six and six or a twelve mile limit was before the conferences in Geneva. These conferences met in 1958 and 1960, and on the last occasion we came very close to bringing about the establishment by international agreement of a six and six mile area territorial sea. We lost out I think by only one vote. Since then no progress has been made in this regard. We have endeavoured to secure agreement among the nations which voted favourably with regard to the establishment of a universal agreement on a new territorial sea area. We have not achieved it. To act unilaterally, however, is one of those things that has dangerous implications, and I know the hon. gentleman and those associated with him while he was in office realized what they are.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ANSWER TO ORDER FOR RETURN
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EXTENSION OF TERRITORIAL WATERS
speechtext: I have a supplementary question. Admitting, of course, the desirability of doing these things by international action if possible, is the Prime Minister not aware of the fact that because of the failure of international action, other countries have taken national action in this regard?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ANSWER TO ORDER FOR RETURN

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EXTENSION OF TERRITORIAL WATERS
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I am certainly aware of that fact. That happened during the period when the hon. gentleman was in office as well, that other countries took action. But we are in a position when we take this action, as the hon. gentleman knows, that our markets in the United States for fisheries may be in danger.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, November 15, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-78, to amend the Income Tax Act- Mr. Nowlan-Mr. Chown in the chair.
On clause 10-Production incentive deduction.

Mr. Chairman, last evening when the committee adjourned I had mentioned that I, and most members of the house, were in favour of production incentives and basically in favour of anything which could be done by way of taxation to encourage manufacturers and other persons in our economy to increase productivity and create new jobs for Canadians.
However, I also pointed out that there are several difficulties involved in clause 10. One of the difficulties I mentioned was that it encourages firms to raise prices in order to get a tax advantage. I pointed out that by raising prices they could create additional income which would be taxable at a lower rate than that normally imposed on the profits of Canadian firms. I pointed out also that there was no incentive to efficiency contained in this clause, in that firms who maintained their selling price at the same level as last year, and who cut down on their production expenses, might have higher profits but would have to pay taxes on those profits at the ordinary rates of taxation rather than the incentive rate envisaged by this clause.
Furthermore, this clause does nothing for the manufacturer who operated at capacity in 1981, who is operating his business efficiently and selling as much as he can. There is no incentive included in this particular

Income Tax Act
clause for him. In addition, this clause encourages the transfer of sales from one company to another by devious means to take advantage of the rates of taxation allowed under this clause of the bill.
I maintained, Mr. Chairman, that this clause does not create incentives which are important enough to cause any real expansion in economic activity. The minister pointed out in his example that if a firm had a $100,000 increase in sales there would be a tax saving of only some $1,200. This, of course, might be more, depending on the increased profit which was generated through the additional $100,000 in sales.
One other important point with respect to this clause which I would like to draw to the attention of the committee is that it leaves out entirely unincorporated manufacturers, and when introducing the budget resolutions last spring the former minister of finance indicated to the house that unincorporated manufacturing concerns were not important. I maintain that many manufacturing concerns develop from rather small beginnings, and that every incentive which is given to the larger concerns should be given to the small men who want to get into manufacturing and who may not go into it through a corporation initially. These people, when they get into manufacturing in a small way, create jobs for Canadians and on occasion grow into important business enterprises. Many of our manufacturing concerns were originally small concerns which started out as an individual or group of individuals who were not incorporated as a limited liability company. Those of us on this side of the house say the small manufacturer is important, and I believe he should be given the same incentive as incorporated companies under this particular clause of the bill.
Aside from these general criticisms of this clause I would like to bring out a few points respecting its wording which I think will cause concern to the government and create litigation in the tax field, and all of us know there is enough litigation in this field now without putting a section into the act which will be very difficult to interpret and administer. Clause 1 of the proposed new section 40A says in part:
There may be deducted from the tax otherwise payable for a taxation year by a manufacturing and processing corporation...
It goes on to outline the amount which may be deducted, and subclauses 2 and 3 go on to say:
"manufacturing and processing corporation" means a corporation that had net sales...
-and so on, from the sale ofgoods processed or manufactured [DOT]..

So we have here a definition of manufacturing and processing, and I would think under the incentives which are given in this particular instance the effect will be that everyone is going to try to be classified as a manufacturing and processing concern, even those who are not ordinarily involved in this type of activity. For example, they will assemble products on their own rather than have them sent to them in completed form.
The minister, who was formerly minister of national revenue, should recall the difficulties he had in determining what were manufacturing and processing concerns under the Excise Tax Act. There were a great many difficulties involved. Under that particular act the minister had discretion to decide what was a manufacturing and processing concern, but under this clause in this bill he will not have that discretion. The Income Tax Act has very few instances of ministerial discretion in it. Perhaps under some provision the minister will be able to determine what is a manufacturing and processing corporation, but in my brief perusal of the bill I could not find such a provision. Subclause 3 of this clause brings into manufacturing many mining and refining companies, because it goes on to state:
The principle business of a corporation for a taxation year shall be deemed to be mining, operating an oil or gas well or a combination of both if
(i)	its profits . . . are at least 50 per cent of
(ii)	the amount that would be its income for the year if no amount were deductible, in computing its income for the year . . .
and so on. This means, I think, that some mining corporations will benefit from this clause. At the time the legislation was introduced in the former budget resolutions last spring we were not led to believe that mining corporations were to receive the benefits of this particular clause of the bill, and I believe that under the bill, as it is presently written, they will obtain advantages which were not foreseen when the budget resolutions were brought in last spring.
Subclause 4 of this clause says that:
"Subsection (1) -
That is the one that allows the tax deductions:
-does not apply in the case of a manufacturing and processing corporation that did not carry on business for at least 12 months immediately preceding the taxation year referred to in subsection (1) in respect of which the tax is otherwise payable.
This means that if some people are thinking of going into manufacturing they will not get the benefit of this particular clause in the first year of their operations. This may mean that they will choose to operate within the corporate organization in a small way in the first year, and then move sales from an

unincorporated body into it in the second year in order to get the full advantage of the tax reductions provided in this bill.
In subclause 7 of the proposed section 40A the term "connected corporation" is used. Basically a corporation is a body corporate created by a group of people getting together and forming a company in order to obtain the advantages of limited liability, and perhaps for other purposes; but under the Income Tax Act we find we have "personal corporations" "related corporations" "associated corporations" and now we are having "successor corporations". I am sure schemes will be devised to avoid being a connected corporation, just as they have been devised to avoid two corporations being associated or related, or a corporation being a personal corporation.
In effect I think this sort of legislation encourages people to try to find ways to get around it, because there is a specific tax advantage if you are not a successor corporation. If you are a manufacturing corporation, tax lawyers and other people engaged in taxation matters for corporations can find ways to get around sections of the act so they can fit people into its provisions in order to get tax advantages, and by so doing in some cases they can under this section manage to have taxation reduced by as much as 50 per cent. In all cases there will be a tax reduction of 25 per cent for new corporations which can be created within the meaning of the terms of this clause in the bill.
In the definition in subclause 8 it is stated:
...a manufacturing and processing corporation is connected in a taxation year with another corporation.. .if.. .the connected corporation purchased goods from the manufacturing and processing corporation in the year equal in amount to at least 50 per cent of the manufacturing and processing corporation's net sales...
I am sure there will be sales of 49 per cent of products to avoid this term being applied, and other ways will be found to fit corporations within the provisions of this particular clause.
Subclause 9 is the final subclause in this clause, and is intended to be the one which will prevent sales being transferred in order to take advantage of this clause in the bill. However, I believe it is ineffective, because it indicates that the primary purpose of the transfer of sales must be to take advantage of this clause. It is difficult enough to determine "purposes" without trying to determine "primary purposes" and I think there will be many legal arguments, where sales are transferred to a particular corporation, on the question of whether or not the primary purpose of the transfer of these sales is to take advantage of this clause in the bill.

In summary I think this particular clause of the act, although the idea of incentives is good, does not go far enough. I think it is very poorly drawn. It is drawn in such a way that it is going to encourage additional tax litigation, and it is going to cause the government introducing it and the courts a great deal of worry in the future. It is, further, going to encourage people to devise means of getting around the Income Tax Act. I think that legislation which does this is poor legislation.

Mr. Chairman, speaking in practical and non-technical terms, which the minister and I both understand, the incentive legislation which has been introduced under his auspices, but with the co-operation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to stimulate increased sales will, as I said last night, in my submission be ineffective in achieving what it is aimed at achieving, for two practical reasons. The first is that while resolution No. 2 was a very simple paragraph with very simple objects, the legislation as it is drafted, with over six pages here, is so complicated and the potential tax saving so minimal-and I refer again to the minister's own example in the income tax bill-that my fear is that the average manufacturing corporation will not undergo the risk and expense of retaining the necessary accounting and legal advice to come squarely under this section to achieve what after all is a very minimal, or proportionately very minimal, tax saving.
The second feature is that because of the moveable sales base that there is in this clause, the success of a manufacturing or processing operation in year one in increasing its sales will automatically increase the sales base and penalize that company in year two. In other words, after one good year the corporation is probably deprived of any benefit of the legislation in succeeding years. For those two practical reasons I suggest once again to the minister that the results which are honestly sought by this particular amendment will, in our opinion at least, not be achieved.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister made it reasonably clear last evening that this legislation was introduced before he became Minister of Finance. I thought it might be helpful to look up some of the explanations given by his predecessor when he introduced these resolutions. I would like to read a few words from pages 2703 and 2704 of Hansard for April 10 in which the

Income Tax Act
previous minister oi finance described the reasons and purposes of this and the other resolutions:
One of the new measures is expressly designed as an incentive for further industrial expansion and increased employment.
Then he goes on to say, on this and the resolution on research:
They will constitute an important addition to the structure of tax changes which I have brought to this house in recent years. Encouragement and incentive are thus being given to private industry under several related headings, to increase its efficiency, to expand employment, to improve Canada's competitive position and to keep current with the most advanced technical and scientific methods.
In the next paragraph he goes on to say that a number of these resolutions or changes "result from probing into the deficiencies of the tax system in a continuing effort to overcome obstacles to progress and to achieve greater equity among taxpayers".
If that is the purpose, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that this particular proposal fails dismally to meet that objective, because in the first place the incentives are very meagre; in the second place, as was pointed out before, they will result in certain windfall profits resulting to companies because of the devaluation of the dollar which, as the minister said yesterday, was not contemplated at the time these proposals were made. Taxpayers will receive a benefit, a bonus or an incentive for increasing prices. This, surely, is the very opposite of what this legislation should be trying to achieve. If, for instance, perhaps because of the tariff surcharges, companies are in a position to increase prices, instead of being condemned for doing that and taking advantage of these increased surcharges, they are going to be bonused for it.
It seems to me those are reasons which make this particular incentive bonus a very questionable piece of legislation. I would like to ask the minister whether there is any way in which taxpayers who do increase prices for some of the reasons that have been mentioned in the house will be prevented from taking advantage of the tax incentives that are offered in this clause.

Mr. Chairman, I think this is another of those clauses which give incentives to producers and corporations to encourage them to produce, whereas what is needed, in our opinion, is more incentive to the consumer to enable him to be in a position to consume. In line with that, I think if we look to the south we will find that the United States provides very much more generous incentives to the taxpayers of that country than we do here, on a consumer

basis. I have read that there are now more persons of Canadian descent living in the United States than there are Canadians living in Canada. If this is true, I think we must look to the difference between our tax system and that in the United States which makes it so attractive for so many of our Canadian people to go there rather than live here.
It might be useful, Mr. Chairman, to consider one or two of the distinctions which are apparent in the United States income tax exemptions as they affect the consuming public, as compared to those we have in Canada. There is, for example, instalment buying. When you purchase property of any kind on the instalment plan in the United States you may deduct the interest payments from your income tax. Such property includes automobiles, television sets, radios and home furnishings of all types. Also deductible are the interest portions of home mortgage payments. This represents a very substantial saving to the taxpaying consumer in the United States, and encourages many people to build or buy their own homes. I think the same could be said for those clauses which exempt interest payments on home furnishings such as those I have mentioned. In addition, in the United States taxpayers are exempt from paying income taxes on real estate and personal property. State income taxes are all-
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, has this reference to clause 10, which I think deals with incentives to business on the basis of increased sales?
Mr. Chairman, I know the clause intends to do that, but my argument is that I do not think we are doing it in this measure.

In fairness to the hon.
member, Mr. Chairman, I might say that we are having difficulty hearing him. If he would speak directly into the microphone perhaps we would hear him better.

speechtext: Order. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

The point raised by the hon. member was whether what I was saying had reference to clause 10. My contention is that it has, because I oppose the ideas expressed in clause 10. I contend that they would give incentive to the producers, the corporations, to urge them to produce, whereas what is needed in Canada, in my opinion, is more incentive to be given to the consumer in order to help him consume.
In line with that, I said that in the United States many more generous concessions or inducements to the consumer are given under their tax structure. I think this has been a great inducement to many Canadians to leave our country and go to the United States. It may be unfortunate, but I believe this is one of the facts of life which has attracted people there. In this connection I have read, and I think it is pretty close to the truth, that there are now more persons of Canadian descent living in the United States than there are in Canada. I believe that if our tax system was more realistic and gave better recognition to the needs of the common people of Canada, this situation would not exist. I cited a few instances of the more generous terms given under the United States tax structure to their consumers, and among them were these. There is one which exempts-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not want to be unduly restrictive as far as the remarks of the hon. member are concerned. I know one can do this sort of thing by way of analogy and
Income Tax Act
therefore still tightrope-walk the rule of relevancy. But I just want to caution him, and we will continue to hear what he has to say. I hope his remarks will come within the strict rule, and it is a strict rule in committee.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is hard on me. When you could not hear what I was saying, you did not like it; now you do hear what I say, and you still do not like it. In view of your ruling, sir, which certainly I abide by though I think it is a little harsh, may I say that I have about another two minutes to outline my ideas and then I will conclude. Those ideas are, in the main, that the incentives should be given to the consumers, not to the producers.
In conclusion, in regard to the examples I quoted from the United States of how they give incentives to consumers, may I say that in that country the following taxes and charges are exempt from federal income tax. They exempt real estate, personal property and state income taxes. Poll taxes are deductible. Auto licenses and registration fees, casualty and theft losses are deductible. Work clothes in cases of employment demanding special apparel are deductible. Certain types of personal transportation expenses are deductible. Educational expenses are also deductible when incurred primarily for maintaining or improving skills involved in a person's employment.
Mr. Chairman, that is all I have to say in brief. I reiterate the idea, which our party has long put forward, that what we need in Canada are more incentives to the consumer to help him consume and less to the corporations to help them, possibly, to produce but more likely to make additional profits.

In connection with clause 10 I just want to make some reference to exporters. Under this clause exporters can benefit even though they do not increase their volume of sales. In fact they can benefit even though their volume of sales is down by 3 per cent or 4 per cent. But if our dollar should stay depressed at, say, 92J cents for a year or so, their sales base would be high, and our exporters would not benefit until they had an increase in export sales of about or close to 10 per cent.
The whole purpose of this clause is to increase the volume of business. I should think it would be within the ingenuity of the minister's department to include a clause to eliminate the effect of the variation in the value of the Canadian dollar as far as computing income tax of corporations is concerned. There is nothing in the clause now to allow that. As an example, if the Canadian dollar was down by an average of 5 per cent in the year

Income Tax Act
as compared to the previous year, then 5 per cent of the export sales abroad would not or should not count as an increase in business for income tax purposes. I think we could also make provision in the Income Tax Act for an increase in sales when our dollar was going up in value.
The whole purpose of this clause is to increase volume of sales, to increase production in our country; and it seems to me that we are extending the benefits at a time when our dollar is depressed and it is easier to sell our products, and we are making it harder to sell our products when our dollar goes up in value.

Mr. Chairman, nothing is sure but death and taxes, they say, but I am delighted to see a reduction in taxes coming up. I was wondering whether the Minister of Finance has taken into account the operation of a new industry starting up initially in this coming year. Normally a new industry needs a respectable cash flow, but these incentive agreements in this clause mean that the owner of such an industry will be paying the full rate on any profit in the first year of business. Normally the growth rate of a business does not go up in a straight line, and particularly in the export field there are a great number of firms entering it for the first time who are operating on a loss position until they initiate a marketing capability in a foreign area.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance, Mr. Chairman, that some consideration should be given to a firm starting up in business and an accelerated depreciation allowed to that firm in the first year of business in lieu of a tax credit which is available in the succeeding year after the initial operation, so that the money can be retained in the business and not go out of the business in tax dollars. As I have suggested, in the formative years of a business the first year in a lot of cases is very critical in regard to cash flow.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I could say to the Minister of Finance, in regard to this clause dealing with production incentives, that we have had pointed out that all this purports to do is to make a slight variation in the cost curve. If we are thinking of incentives, then probably the real consideration should be demand curves, although the two must obviously be considered together. But when we think of the timing of this legislation, I note that the budget, of which this is a part, was brought down on April 10 last, and at that time I submit that the government had no real knowledge that there would be a dollar devaluation. I say that with some confidence because on March 21, 1962, I asked the then

minister of finance if he had given consideration to establishing a pegged rate, and the minister's reply was:
The house has been kept well informed on the very striking success of the government's policy in relation to the external value of the Canadian dollar.
From that answer which was given on March 21, 1962, I take it that the government, when they brought in their budget on April 10, were thinking in terms of a dollar of approximately 95 cents. Then on April 10 we have the production incentives proposal, which is obviously going to give very considerable benefit to anybody who can establish higher cost sales or higher sales on a cost basis. Let me give this illustration, and it is hypothetical, of course; a newsprint company that has perhaps contracted for the sale of $1 million tons of newsprint, let us say to the Wall Street Journal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wish they would do so.
I do not know the facts. I am sure the minister would know who are benefiting. I am sure he knows who is benefiting by this extraordinary legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Our balance of payments.

Yes. In any event I ask the minister to hear me with patience. I am suggesting that a good many people who have benefited from the devaluation forced on this government on May 3, 1962, in extremis, are really people who are satisfying an inelastic demand curve. In other words, the fact that there is a price change is not going to alter the content of volume shipped, for instance, of newsprint. Therefore we have this newsprint company which is going to ship exactly the same requirements now that they shipped previously but they get the additional advantage of the devaluation on May 3, 1962, and on top of that they get this additional gift of a bonus with respect to a substantial tax cutback, not because they ship one more ton of paper but merely because this government has given them the bonus on the bonus.
We have in mind the fact that since this government has been in power the national debt per employed person has increased by $321. I may say I am going by these figures. In 1957 the national debt per employed person was $1,923. In 1962 it is up to $2,244. In this respect I think we have a good deal of sympathy with some of our friends on the left who talk in terms of consumption, because these additional debt charges are purely moneys that are going to be paid by Canadians and ultimately by Canadian consumers. This is what they mean. Hence actually what is

happening suddenly, by even this clause here, is a shift from, I would say, progressive taxation in effect to regressive taxation.
I do not think there is any possibility that this can provide a solution. Those parts of the community that have been most benefited by devaluation-and many people will have been benefited by this action-in many instances are going to get the extra bonus. Those people who have been benefited by the devaluation of May 3, 1962 are going to get this bonus out of the pockets of other Canadian people. The objections that have been presented by some of the members of the New Democratic party in this house have pointed out quite accurately and truthfully that actually the benefits to one must be paid for by the loss to the other.
I think it is only fair that the minister answer fairly and accurately who is going to benefit, in his view, from these production incentives already involved. I think he should answer this question. If the government had known that devaluation would be forced on it on May 3, 1962, would it have ever countenanced section 10 with its production incentive in this particular form? For example, when studying the tax structures of western Europe at the present time, we know perfectly well that many things have been done by Germany, Belgium, France, Italy and other countries which have produced all kinds of production incentives. However, I submit that what we have here in clause 10 has failed, is already out of date and obsolete. Even to permit it to pass in this form is adding an injustice to something that has already taken place as a result of the collapse of our dollar.

I have been seeking to catch your eye, Mr. Chairman, in order to raise two matters, one of which is in the general area which was under discussion by the preceding speaker and which in my opinion was pinpointed by the hon. member for Welland in particular. It relates to this matter of the devaluation of the dollar. If our dollars were fluctuating freely the minister might argue that this was an irrelevant discussion. However, it seems to me that when the Canadian dollar is pegged as a matter of government policy, this question is then very relevant to the clause under discussion.
The minister has already suggested that these proposals were contained in the budget of last April and that he is bringing them forward, as I understood it, virtually intact. However, in the light of all that has transpired since that time, and particularly in relation to the government action in pegging the dollar, I suggest that there would have
Income Tax Act
been plenty of opportunity for the government to have another look at this question. If we are going to proceed with this sort of plan I believe that the distinction which is drawn by the hon. member for Welland, between manufacturers who are producing for the domestic market and corporations which are primarily engaged in the export market is valid.
I certainly know this. From all recent reports that have come from the large manufacturing and processing corporations in British Columbia which are engaged in the export trade, their financial returns as a result of the devaluation of the dollar have been quite substantial, to say the least. I think the illustration with respect to newsprint exports was a good one, and that with this proposal they are going to get another kick at the cat and in a way which is not, as far as I can see, going to provide another job in, for example, the forest products industry of British Columbia. I think this is a matter to which the minister should give some reply.
There is another part of this clause in respect of which I should like to have a reply from him. I refer to subclause 2 in particular, in line 32, where it goes into the matter of defining what is meant by "manufacturing and processing corporation" for the purposes of this clause. It uses the words
-but does not include a corporation whose principal business for the year was-
And then it enumerates a number of categories. First of all I should like to inquire on what basis the determination is going to be made with respect to what is the principal business of a corporation. I raise this point with particular reference to the fact that one of the excluded processes is logging, and having in mind that in a later clause of the bill there is a special provision with reference to logging and the taxation of profits on logging.
The forest products industry of British Columbia, which happened to be the type of manufacturing and processing corporation with which I am most familiar, includes logging as well as the production of manufactured products. When the minister replies I should like him to use that industry as an example of how it is going to be determined whether the principal business of corporations like B.C. Forest Products, Crown Zeller -bach or MacMillan, Bloedel, Powell River is logging or whether it is not for purposes of this clause. If we are going to proceed with this clause in this form I am wondering whether, in view of the other clause in the bill, we will not have amended the act in a way which will in effect segregate the profits of a corporation from logging from those derived from manufacturing and processing. As

Income Tax Act
I understand this clause and the one which we will be considering later, I can see a real possibility that some of these large export corporations are not only going to have two kicks at the cat but a third kick at the cat under the provisions of the later clause.
I certainly would appreciate some explanation from the minister of just what is involved in the determination of what is the principal business, and I should also like to hear him comment on the discussion in which we have been engaged with regard to the relationship of this proposal to the devaluation of the dollar.

Mr. Chairman, if I thought the minister could use the next five minutes before lunch to deal in full with the criticisms that have been advanced with respect to this clause I would not speak now, but we are dealing with a very serious matter, in that it was indicated by the former minister of finance when he advanced this proposal that it involved the major part of the tax concessions in the budget and, indeed, involved a tax abatement or a tax value estimated at $88 million, I believe.
I would be interested in knowing whether the new minister and his officials would now suggest to the committee that that figure is just as valid now as it was in April, inasmuch as they have had so many months between then and now to consult with those in industry and manufacturing who may benefit. I would imagine that the figure was more or less of a guess in April, but I would think that as a result of their negotiations with the taxpayers affected they might now want to come up with some revision.
As I indicated last night, I have never claimed to be an expert with regard to this complicated act. However, we now have in the house several chartered accountants from whom we have heard, and last night and today we also heard from members who to my personal knowledge devote a good deal of their legal practice to tax work. I am sure the minister has been impressed with the suggestions that as drafted this particular proposal, good as I know it was intended to be, offers unusual loopholes, windfalls and opportunities for tax avoidance that I know it is never the intention of the department to permit. On Wednesday last I read, as no doubt many other members did, the very interesting daily financial column of John Meyer in the Montreal Gazette, and I was struck by these words:
The biggest poker game in Canada today is tax avoidance.
It would appear that in an unusual way this particular clause is providing a wider opportunity for tax avoidance which, as has

been pointed out, is a legitimate exercise. When the crown presents legislation it is up to it to make sure that it is not in the nature of a sieve for tax avoidance, and in these difficult days of high taxation a taypayer has every right to employ experts in a legitimate way to find loopholes if they exist in the legislation.
Therefore our concern is to get an answer from the minister with respect to the criticism of this clause. We have always suggested that to stimulate business in these difficult times, with the unemployment we have had in the last four or five years, we certainly need all the incentives for increased production and employment that ingenuity can present to us, but this clause does not seem to be it. While this clause was perhaps rather hurriedly devised in the election atmosphere of last April, a number of months have since gone by, and it would seem to me that there is some lack of ingenuity on the part of the administration inasmuch as they learned at the polls that their proposals were not very popular, as indicated by the return of a much smaller number of members of their party to this house. Having that in mind, I should have thought they would have presented a new budget, not something, as I said last night, simply representing a warming up of what even last April was only a halfbaked proposal not properly thought through.
As the minister has had since last night to do some homework and prepare himself to explain how these loopholes are taken care of, and as I have made it possible for him to have another hour and a half to consider the very important criticisms that have been advanced this morning, I hope the minister will be full of information as to what is contained in the bill that will prevent the happening of the things that have been predicted by so many members this morning.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When the committee rose at one o'clock we were dealing with clause 10. Shall clause 10 carry?
I wonder if the Minister of Finance might answer some of the questions that have been raised in respect of this clause before we move on to the other clauses in the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I expected to try to answer some of the questions which have been raised, but I thought it would facilitate matters if we had most of them before us at the time rather than answer them individually. It was for this reason I was waiting until all the questions were before the committee. I suppose the committee would like to have some of the matters discussed which have been raised by hon. gentlemen opposite. I must say that I feel this has been an interesting, and I think an informative, debate. With all due respect to hon. gentlemen who participated in it, I must say frankly that I have not heard any questions raised during last evening and this morning that I have not heard raised during the consultations in respect of this bill.
I realize there are difficulties in connection with it. I realize there are difficulties in connection with administration. I realize some of the problems which are raised by this measure. I would suggest this situation could arise in connection with any amendment or any change in a taxation statute. This is perhaps a new approach, in one sense of the word, and therefore there may be fields opened up which were not opened up in other taxation statutes. The government had given very careful consideration to most of these criticisms, at any rate, but not the details of them. We realized that these problems existed, but we felt it advisable to go ahead with this measure because, as my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce said yesterday afternoon, there has been a substantial demand from manufacturers and producers in Canada for this measure. Despite some of the criticisms which I think are justified, and notwithstanding some of the difficulties which are fairly 27507-3-109
Income Tax Act
obvious in connection with this measure, I believe it will do a substantial amount of good for the manufacturing industry of this country. We are, therefore, proceeding on that basis.
This morning I was asked who were going to benefit from this legislation. Well, of course, all exporters who increase their exports are going to benefit from this legislation. Manufacturers who increase their production over the base year are going to benefit from it. There should be, and it is anticipated there will be, a substantial increase in employment in this country. This is the basic design of this legislation.
Now, it has been said that there are windfalls connected with this legislation which my friends suggest result from the devaluation of the dollar. The fact that this was an unexpected windfall, it was suggested, should add substantially to the profits of certain phases of industry. In the first place, Mr. Chairman, it must be emphasized that if there is a windfall it only accrues to the export trade because the exporters are the ones who will get the advantage of the devaluation of the dollar. So far as I am concerned, quite frankly, if I can help increase the exports of this country and thereby help to offset the balance of payments problem, which is one of the fundamental problems facing this nation, then I am not going to worry unduly at the inception of legislation about possible accruals of benefit to exporters.
This is a matter which will always, of course, be under review. This statute is not one which runs in perpetuity and is unchangeable like the laws of the Medes and the Persians. This act is before parliament every year and is open to review and amendment. I do suggest this matter of windfall benefit is one which, if there is a windfall, accrues only to the exporter. While there has been a substantial increase in our exports, we certainly need to assist that aspect of our trade in every way possible.
As the hon. member for Leeds, I think, pointed out this morning, when this budget was introduced by my predecessor in April, the dollar was then at 95. The fiscal years of corporations have been closing at various times since then, so the result is not necessarily a windfall of 7.5 cents on the dollar. It may be, at the most, 2.5 cents on the dollar. In any event, as I have said, so far as the government is concerned, we are prepared to stand on this basis if this is of assistance to exporters. If there is a windfall there, the advantage which may accrue to them is not such as would deter the government from proceeding with the legislation; in fact, it is something which would encourage it.

Income Tax Act
It has been suggested by someone, I think the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, that the advantages which were going to accrue were infinitesimal, negligible and of very little benefit to most exporters or manufacturers. This was one phase of the argument. Then, the hon. member for Davenport and other gentlemen who have taken part in this debate have suggested that there might be substantial profits accruing as a result of this measure. Well, you cannot have it both ways, Mr. Chairman, that the results will be negligible and there will be no substantial profits, and that there is going to be a bonus, as some of my hon. friends have stressed. In order to achieve this tax avoidance, as pointed out by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, it would be necessary to have corporate re-organization. There would be substantial legal costs involved, and at least his argument was an answer to that.
I point out too that, if as has been suggested, it is possible to raise prices in one year and thereby attract a profit which would result in this tax benefit. This is a moving feature. It moves on from one year to another and if something of that nature should be done in one year it means that the next year the taxpayer would be in a very difficult situation indeed and would not derive the benefit from the so-called increase, artificial or otherwise, created the year before.
I do not necessarily accept the fact that this would be done because, as my colleague pointed out yesterday afternoon, although somebody has said this is an entirely free competitive economy, we all must admit that there are various features about it which do not quite meet the picture Adam Smith had of the economy a century ago. Competition still plays a very substantial part in our economy, particularly in our mercantile world, and I am not too concerned with that when one considers the statutory provisions which are in here now, and also the law of competition.
I am not going to worry the committee by recounting all the amendments and provisions in the bill, but there are substantial ones which will effectively prevent any taxpayer escaping or using this legislation in an attempt to defraud the revenue.
I was also asked by an hon. member this morning who would decide whether it was processing and manufacturing, and he pointed out that the Minister of National Revenue does not now have any great discretion in these matters. That is perfectly true although there was a time when he did have very substantial discretion. However, a prudent government in its wisdom saw fit to decide that
[Mr. Nowlan.)
most of those discretionary powers should be removed and that matters be left to the courts to decide.
Although the Minister of National Revenue may not have great discretionary power I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite who discussed the bill today will agree, from experience, that we have a very able group of expert officials in the Department of National Revenue, and if a taxpayer submits a return and is claiming something under this bill, or pursuant to this legislation, although the minister may not have a great lot of discretionary power certainly he and his department have the discretion of saying no and disallowing items which the taxpayer claims. The taxpayer can then either accept the revision or reassessment of the department or go to the income tax appeal board or the exchequer court, or indeed both as he sees fit.
That is one of the effective mechanisms which is always there and which will guard against the anticipated abuses which may arise out of this legislation. I would remind hon. members that abuses have arisen out of other sections. These abuses are known to departmental officials, as my hon. friends opposite are well aware, and I believe the department can decide fairly effectively what steps should be taken to prevent those abuses arising.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni raised a technical point this morning with respect to one definition in the bill. However, provision has been in the Income Tax Act for many years-I think it is section 83A-covering that point, and I do not anticipate there will be any great difficulty whatsoever with respect to it.
It has also been pointed out that small corporations may not benefit too much by the provisions of this bill. However I think small corporations will benefit to a substantial degree, and I need not point out to the committee that the tax benefits accruing to small corporations have been increased on two occasions since this government came into power in 1957, during which time the income bracket subject to the lower rate went from $20,000 to $35,000. That in itself provided fairly substantial assistance to the small corporations.
The question was also asked why individuals, who were unincorporated, were not included in this provision. The reason must be obvious to any hon. gentleman conversant with the tax law because taxation on an individual is, of course, on a graduated scale while taxation on a corporation is on a flat basis, and it is easier to give 50 per cent or 25 per cent deductions in the case of corporations than it is in the case of individuals.

One individual may have a tax rate of 80 per cent and a border line individual may have a tax rate of 30 so hon. members can readily see the inequalities that would arise. This phase of the matter was given very careful consideration at a time when I was minister of national revenue and we decided it would be absolutely impractical to make a provision such as that because it would be impossible to administer. That is why the deduction is left on the corporate basis.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, or some other hon. member opposite, pointed out that there was no benefit to a company starting in its first year. It was said that many companies had difficulties in getting under way and that therefore it was perhaps unfair not to allow a benefit to such companies. That is doubtlessly true; but on the other hand if there is going to be tax avoidance, if there is going to be this splitting up, or these semi-illegal arrangements which have been suggested by the hon. member for Davenport and others, then it is advisable to take that into consideration. The bill does this by providing that these tax benefits shall not accrue to a company in its first year.
I think this answers most of the criticisms made of the legislation. As I say, Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the manner in which the debate has been conducted. I know full well that there are difficulties in connection with this legislation but I also believe there are some substantial benefits connected with the enactment of it. I would hope the committee would see fit to pass this now so that we could go on with the other clauses. I am quite sure if that is done, then beneficial results will accrue to the economy of the country.

I do not want to review and rehash all the things already said about this legislation, but I would like to record that the minister's explanations and answers to our questions have been anything but clear and precise. They covered certain ground that we did not cover, ground of a more political nature, but there is one thing in particular which he said and on which I wish to comment. He suggested that if there was anything wrong with this legislation then in some mysterious way the very efficient officials of the Department of National Revenue could do something about it. The trouble with bad law is that officials cannot do anything about it. This is bad law and in my humble opinion it will not do the things that have been represented on its behalf.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 10 carry?

Mr. Chairman, I simply want to say a word on the other side of the coin. Up to now we have been discussing 27507-3-109J
Income Tax Act
the question of whether or not this statute is properly and tightly drawn to prevent the maximum of tax avoidance. Also, the question has been before us as to whether this is the best way to provide business incentives, assuming that we have $88 million of tax abatement as a means of doing it. The minister says critics of his formulas cannot have it both ways. We pointed out that this may not be the best way of providing these incentives. It has been suggested that price increases would provide various windfalls and there would be other means by which benefits would accrue without perhaps being earned in the way of incentive, which this clause was designed to provide.
There is another side to the coin. It is that this particular remedy as compared with, say, depreciation allowances or some other form of incentive to industry, would be ineffective if prices go down, and go down to the extent that no matter how hard the producer works, no matter how hard he tries to and perhaps does increase his production, he may not increase his production in dollars under this formula in a manner that would entitle him to get tax benefit.
This is not something that is hypothetical. I am sure the minister read, as I read last week, in the Financial Post the lead headline to their editorial, which is "The big threat in price trends". They quote perhaps the greatest authority in the world today, Per Jacobsson, the managing director of the international monetary fund. He was right a few months ago when people were worried about inflation when he said that was not our concern. But now he gives us rather ominous warnings and, to quote the Financial Post, the prophecy means that "there is unpleasant evidence that the Canadian stage is set for deflation". The Financial Post says:
Substantial as this year's economic growth may be, it is indeed far from making up for five previous years of stagnation and steadily rising unemployment.
I am not going to take personal responsibility for receiving from the minister, as we in the opposition usually do in debates of this kind, the immediate charge of simply, "You are a prophet of gloom and doom". I am simply going to point out to the minister that concern is being expressed today by reputable independent financial observers, particularly those who speak to us from the financial journals of this country. Just yesterday those of us who subscribe received this week's issue of the Financial Post. The lead headline on the front page is "1963 Prospects Slow Down Sure". I am just pointing out to the minister that this formula is not one that will help business if we are in for deflation.

Income Tax Act
No matter how hard the businessman tries, under this formula in price deflation, though his volume may increase he will not win because his sales have not gone up in gross dollar value.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 12-Logging tax deduction.

Mr. Chairman, as was brought out, of course, in the debate on the resolution, this section is intended to remedy the injustice that exists under the present legislation that is in force in two provinces in Canada, namely British Columbia and Ontario. When the logging tax was first introduced in 1949 in the province of Ontario there was not a great deal of objection taken because it was a resource tax and it was more or less an operating expense. Some four years later similar legislation was passed in British Columbia, and while a protest was raised that it was in effect an increase in income tax, there was no strenuous objection until the year 1957 when both provinces, Ontario and British Columbia, went beyond the stage of taxing the logging operations and began to tax the profits on the operations of the plywood factory, the shingle mill, the saw mill or the other processing units involved. It then became an income tax. But because the dominion-provincial fiscal agreements had been entered into in that year there was not very much that could be done about it until the expiration of the agreements.
I know that since the expiration of the agreements, approximately 18 months ago, continuous representations have been made by operators in all parts of British Columbia and Ontario to the three governments concerned to correct this discrimination, this tax, which results in the forest industries of the two provinces paying a higher income tax than any other units in the forest industry in other parts of Canada. I feel that the government is to be commended for having taken the step to correct this injustice. I might say that when I first saw section 41(A) I was a bit concerned about the wording of subsection 2(a), where it says that the " 'income for the year from logging operations in the province' has the meaning given to that expression by regulation." I was inclined to

fear that possibly the effect of this legislation might be weakened by that. But after discussing it with other colleagues in the house and considering the matter further I must say that, having in mind the action taken by the government of British Columbia earlier this year, probably the government could not have done otherwise than introduce this subsection. Therefore we on this side of the house feel this is remedial legislation correcting an injustice, and we support it.

Mr. Chairman, I have one or two questions I should like to ask the minister on this clause. The argument was advanced, although it was not advanced specifically just now, by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre that this tax has constituted a double taxation on the same income. But when one reads the bill he realizes that perhaps that is not an argument the minister can advance because this bill does not propose to remove it entirely. However, when we examine another document from another place, the report by the government of British Columbia entitled "An economic review of resources, production and government finances" issued in July of 1962 we see this section. This is the part about which I would like to have some information from the minister:
Logging Tax Act (Revised Statutes of British Columbia, 1960, chapter 225, and amendments) - levies a tax of 10 per cent on income derived from logging operations in excess of $25,000. Under the Logging Tax Act Offset Act (B.C.S. 1962, chapter 35) the lieutenant governor in council is authorized by regulation to offset the logging tax against tax payable under the Income Tax Act, 1962-in lieu of the deduction of the logging tax from income under that act-in the ratio of the general provincial corporation to the federal corporation tax. Provincial action on the full offset of the logging tax is conditional on the federal government providing an offset of the logging tax to its general corporation tax in the ratio of the federal corporation tax to the provincial corporation tax (i.e., the province bear nine forty sevenths of the full offset and Canada thirty eight forty sevenths). This proposal would fully remove the burden of the logging tax.
What I should like the minister to tell us is this. Does this mean that the government of Canada has arranged with the government of British Columbia-although the proportions do not seem quite to jibe, because two thirds, if my arithmetic is right, is not quite the same as thirty eight forty sevenths-to agree to remove completely any tax from logging operations as such? Because I think the committee ought to know that. I think there is a certain plausibility, at least, to the argument that there should not be double taxation of the same income; but if it is advanced as a measure of relief for a number of struggling lumber companies, then I am obliged to view

it with a certain amount of misgiving and reserve. It may be that the logging corporations of British Columbia, who are by far the major economic section of the province of British Columbia, are suffering from the dreadful burden of paying $3 million to the provincial treasury in addition to what they pay to the federal treasury. But I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that before we begin to shed too many tears over them, we should examine their balance sheets.
I have before me the figures of an operation which takes place in my own constituency. I am sure it is of great interest to this government too, because the leading figure one hears of in connection with this is that of the new deus ex machina of the Conservative party, who sometimes looms over us from the gallery. This is the British Columbia Forest Products Company. They became well known in British Columbia a few years ago on account of a rather distressing circumstance which resulted in a cabinet minister being sent to the penitentiary for bribery, or rather for being bribed. According to the court action, he was bribed to provide extra forest management rights to this company. In 1958 this was a very struggling little company and made a profit of only $718,943. But in 1959 they were really beginning-as we say in British Columbia-to log, both metaphorically and actually, and there was a profit of $3,224,503. In 1960-and I am sorry this is the last figure I have-the profit had increased to $3,535,044. Of course, there were also other considerations, and they were able to put aside in 1960 some $4 million in depreciation and depletion. This, incidentally, is the company which not long ago was announcing with understandable elation that in the first six months of 1962 their profits had increased by 50 per cent over their profits for the comparable period of 1961. It is generally considered that a large part at least of this increase in profits was due to the action of the government in devaluing the dollar.
Now let us come to another one, and this one I might call the daddy of the lot. It is very dear to the hearts of British Columbians because we have seen it grow like the mighty oak from the small acorn. Some of us in British Columbia are old enough to remember when an extremely eminent public servant in British Columbia, the chief forester of the province, took a trip to Europe at public expense in order to sound out market conditions in Europe. He came back and established an export company which since that time has grown, as I say, like the mighty oak from the small acorn. Now the MacMillan, Bloedel, Powell River Company Limited is
Income Tax Act
able to make quite satisfactory earnings. In 1959 they made a net profit after all costs and all taxes of $23J million. In addition to that, of course, they also tucked away $150,783,000 in depreciation.
Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that if we are going to accede to the principle, which has I admit a certain validity, that there should not be double taxation of the same income, we should at least make sure that the income is being adequately taxed, and I suggest to you that it is far from adequate at the present time when these sorts of profits are being made. As I say, I am not sure what arrangement has been come to between the two governments; whether it means that on the passage of this bill the provincial government has agreed that it will offset all of the rest of the logging tax and they will not be paying any tax, or whether they are still going to pay some tax to the province. Perhaps these companies prefer to deal with the provinces, having had more satisfactory results in dealing with provincial authorities than they would have with the internal revenue department of the federal government. As my colleague from Comox-Alberni remarked a little while ago, this appears to be giving these companies a second or third kick at the cat, as he called it. I assume that the taxpayer of Canada is the cat which he has in mind. It is at least the taxpayer of Canada who is getting kicked for this.
I am surprised at the intense feeling which has apparently been generated in the logging industry over this tax, which in the light of the figures I have put on the record is almost insignificant. I can only presume that they operate on the age-old precept of looking after the nickels and the dollars will look after themselves, and they do not overlook any bets, however small they may be. But I would suggest this, that if we are going to pass this bill then we must look very closely at the corporation tax structure of this country. I suggest that this government would be well advised to consider revising it in the light of having a much more frequent graduation of corporation tax, somewhat on the lines of graduated personal income tax. Because profits like these, in times like these, plus the enormous allowances which this government and the previous administration have been allowing for depreciation and depletion, to my mind constitute an adequate handout to these struggling little companies.
