Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the section under study is a typical example of what we mentioned yesterday to the effect that these tax exemptions aimed at

Income Tax Act
encouraging an increase in production, especially in the field which is now being considered, would have no effect at all. Let us look at the facts, particularly in the case of corporations engaged in logging operations, and we shall see that what prevents an increase in lumber production is certainly not the burden of taxes, but rather a lack of demand from consumers in this field. For some time now it has been mentioned that there is a decrease in some fields such as in the building industry. Well, it is certainly not because of taxes but rather because consumers lack the purchasing power.
So, Mr. Chairman, I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) if in the case of the logging industry it is not rather the lumberman whose needs would be the greatest and whom we should pity instead of thinking of the logging companies. Indeed, we see that in every place where there is a logging industry, the working class which gets the least from the economic system is still the class of lumbermen.
We cannot be against a tax exemption, but we ask the Minister of Finance to think of lumbermen who, here at least, should be helped by his department so that they can enjoy a more pleasant life.

Mr. Chairman, I completely agree with the statements just made by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), but here is what I find in paragraph (a) of section 12:
There may be deducted from the tax otherwise payable by a taxpayer under this part for a taxation year an amount equal to the lesser of
(a) two thirds of any logging tax paid by the taxpayer to the government of a province in respect of income for the year from logging operations in the province;
Whether it is in the province of Quebec, in British Columbia or any other province, the main point is not merely to allow our logging companies to deduct one third or two thirds from their income tax, as set out in paragraph (a), but rather to provide an outlet for their production. What this country needs today is an expansion of trade. All our logging companies are faced with the problem of surplus production. In British Columbia, everything is being done to find new markets, both domestic and foreign, for those products.
The situation is the same in Quebec. The Canadian International Paper, for example, does not know what to do with its wood.
Is it logical to help the CIP increase its production in Quebec when it cannot even

find markets for the products it has in stock? That is no solution or rather it is putting the cart before the horse.
Like the hon. member for Lapointe, I feel that what we need is to find new markets for our products. Yet we have a ready market for them. Giving advantages to the production industry will in no way increase the purchasing power of those who need that wood.
So, instead of reducing the producers' taxes, let us reduce those of our Canadian consumers. In doing so, we will increase their purchasing power and, by the same token, we will enable the logging companies to meet their obligations, even in the taxation field, since companies like Canadian International Paper can pay taxes more easily than city workers. In fact, because of the taxes he has to pay, the small man cannot afford to build himself a house, the construction of which would take care of our wood surplus.
Mr. Chairman, section 12 of the bill should, in my opinion, look after the consumer rather than the producer, because as I said, what we need in Canada is not production but the power to purchase our production.
(Text):

I am intrigued by the suggestion, if I understood it correctly, just put forward by the previous speaker. We have a great deal of production of pulp and paper in our part of the country, including Kleenex, kraft paper and newsprint. All I can say to the hon. member is that we would really have to pump prime the Canadian consumer if we were ever going to take care of all that production of Kleenex, kraft paper and newsprint. I can see the Toronto Star coming out with editions of 1,000 pages a day, maybe. Perhaps the hon. member would get his ordinary share of that too.
In connection with the logging tax change I should like to make some remarks somewhat in line with those of my colleague from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. I have been interested for some years in seeing this tax removed. In terms of the total budget it really does not amount to very much. I think it was $3 million last year in British Columbia and about $2 million in Ontario. However, it has been used a great deal by these poor abused corporation presidents always under pressure from a spendthrift government and over-eager and over-zealous trade unions to grab more than their share of the cake. It has always been used by them

as an example of the iniquities and the inequities against which they are obliged to fight. I can remember reading some remarks by another colleague of the colleague who is now advising the Minister of Finance. Not only does this adviser who sometimes sits in our presence, but unrecognized, have an influence out in British Columbia; he has influence I suppose throughout the rest of Canada. But even up in northern Ontario two extremely large pulp and paper complexes seem to have come somewhat under his control.
One of these gentlemen, namely Mr. Warwick Fox of the St. Lawrence Paper Corporation, every year when he brings out the annual report, usually takes the opportunity to talk about the iniquity of the welfare state and how false the politicians are in going after more and more money from these corporations which create jobs and which in essence are really rather benevolent institutions.
This logging tax is used by people like Mr. Fox and Mr. Ambridge of Abitibi, and by other companies, as a terrible example. I can remember reading not too long ago where Mr. Ambridge was speaking. Every year he calls in his employees or representatives from unions, at least, and has a bit of a management-labour conference with them. It is a good idea and it goes very well; but almost invariably at these conferences Mr. Ambridge, who is a very canny man, gets rolling, and this logging tax is one of the things he likes to bring forward as the vicious kind of thing that politicians come up with in order to make life miserable and terrible for those great contributors to our economy, the pulp and paper companies.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say it is wonderful that we are finally going to get rid of this iniquitous logging tax, even though it does not represent that much money, as it is going to take something away from the social scene in which the presidents of large wood corporations operate. It is going to take away from them one of their best bleats, and I think that is a very good thing.
Further than that, as long as this tax remains in existence, or the duplication of the tax, we have a confusion within the provincial scene of just what revenue is available and is coming to the provinces from the crown lands which they hold in trust for the people of the province. At least this applies in Ontario and I assume it applies in British Columbia. We have had a tremendous amount of arguing on the provincial scene in Ontario as to just how much revenue we should expect or how much we should take from our natural resource industries.
Income Tax Act
One of the confusions is that so often the person who logs the wood is a great distance away from where the finished product is and where the finished product is sold. We have had the creation of these tremendously large organizations which reach all the way from advertising agencies in the major cities of the world right back to the man cutting the log from the stump. This kind of situation is most confusing where you have in a sense an integrated operation, a very large holding company that may embrace as many as four or five pulp and paper mills and all kinds of side and complementary companies. In this kind of situation it is very difficult to figure out just where the tax money should be taken for both provincial and federal purposes, particularly in relation to the crown lands and the forests which grow on the crown lands. It seems to me that by this move we may be able to have a clearer picture with a little bit less propaganda emanating from the forest industries than we have had in the last few years in Ontario. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I welcome the move that has been made here.
I was interested in the Ontario legislature's Hansard for April 17, 1962. The hon. James Allan, provincial treasurer, was queried about the resolution that the previous minister of finance had just brought in and he made this reply to the questioner:
It is true that logging companies in Ontario have slightly larger taxes to pay, based on income, than an ordinary manufacturing company but it was only on April 10, 1962, that any indication of an adjustment being made by the federal government was introduced when the minister of finance placed on the order paper the following resolution-
Then the resolution is given. Mr. Allan went on to say:
It has been the view of the Ontario government
for years that any duplication of tax that might be deemed to exist should be shared between the federal government and the Ontario government. No evidence that the federal government would share in such a reduction in taxation was indicated until the resolution referred to was introduced in the House of Commons.
If and when this resolution is enacted into law by an amendment to the Income Tax Act of Canada, it is the intention of this government-
The Ontario government.
-to introduce similar legislation to allow a tax credit of one third of the tax on the taxpayer's income from logging operations under the corporations tax act.
That is a verbal assurance by the provincial treasurer in the Ontario house. I wanted to ask the minister if he can give us any indication as to the timing of the probable provincial action or whether he has heard anything to indicate that the province may have changed its mind in relation to this

Income Tax Act
particular promise with regard to taxation revealed by the provincial minister in that speech.
One of the final points I want to touch on in relation to the logging tax has to do with something that the former minister said in his budget speech last spring when he was speaking on this matter. At that time he said that this proposal constitutes a unique concession inasmuch as no other provincial tax is allowed as a deduction under the Income Tax Act. If this is a unique concession, could the minister indicate the reasons why the concession was given? I am not trying to argue against my approval of the move. I should like to know why in this case the federal government is prepared to take a unique step.
I have always understood that the primary rule in setting out a tax policy is never to make an exception if you can possibly help it, and here we have, according to the former minister, a unique concession. I should like to hear from the minister why this is a unique concession and what possible consequences may flow from it. It almost seemed to me as though the former minister was expressing fear that it might open up some other avenues for concession that would be unique. I should like an explanation from the minister not for controversial purposes but just for information.

Mr. Chairman, I rise briefly to express my support of the argument put forward on this clause by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. As a matter of fact, he almost brought tears to my eyes when he was discussing the destitute condition of some of these corporations, which he knows quite well. I am of the personal opinion that there is validity in removing what might be termed a form of double taxation because I think it is an unsound procedure both from the point of view of principle and the point of view of administration.
However, I think it is a wrong approach to suggest that by doing so we are going to relieve a further unnecessary burden upon these large corporations. Under present circumstances, while the profits of these corporations have continued to increase generally speaking over the last three or four years we have had increases in government deficits, increases in difficulties on the part of small businesses and small industry generally throughout Canada, and we have also had an unemployment problem with us continuously. With the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands I believe that we are failing to face up to the opportunities for further revenue when we deal with the problem in

this way. When it comes to the question of this logging tax or other taxes of that type, I have always been of the opinion that the provinces should have resource taxes. They should get their taxes from the value of the timber cut, either stumpage or royalty, from the tons of ore mined and from any other resource used.
Hear, hear.

I am delighted that I am being applauded by the member for Vancouver Centre. I know he has long experience in the forest industry of British Columbia. I have always maintained that as far as revenue is concerned from the operations of those companies that are processing natural resources the provinces should depend upon such a tax.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands gave one or two illustrations of the net profits of certain corporations. He dealt with British Columbia corporations. I have some notes here based on the last information I could obtain. The net profits of the Abitibi Power and Paper Company were $9,657,382 in 1958, nearly $12 million in 1959 and over $12 million in 1960. When we discuss these questions it is not a matter of being personal. I have been informed on good authority that Mr. Ambridge is a very humane, Christian gentleman who has helped many young Canadians over difficult economic stiles. We are dealing with a principle of taxation and the possibilities of further revenue under the circumstances that exist in this country at this time.
Then I come to the Bowater Paper Corporation. Its net profits increased from over $14 million in 1958 to nearly $16 million in 1960 while the net profits of its wholly owned subsidiary, Bowater Corporation of North America Limited, increased from under $9 million in 1958 to over $10 million in 1960. While we support this amendment as tidying up, shall I say, the methods of collecting taxes and removing this degree of double taxation, which is unsound in principle and from the point of view of administration, we believe that under present circumstances we should be giving consideration to securing increasing revenue from these large corporations. It is obvious from their balance sheets that they can well afford to make a greater contribution to the exchequer of this country. We are eliminating this double taxation but at the same time we should do more to compensate small industries and small businesses for the difficulties they are experiencing at the present time. When the minister replies I should like him to give his opinion of the

suggestion we have put forward with relation to increasing the corporation taxes of those corporations that can well afford to pay, and also his opinion with respect to the taxation of resources within the jurisdiction of the provinces.

Before the minister speaks, may I say I would not want hon. members or others who might read our proceedings to gather that the members on this side of the house are speaking on behalf of some 10 or 12 large pulp and paper companies. What the last four speakers all seem to have overlooked is that there are several hundred manufacturers of forest products throughout the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia who are seriously affected by this tax. It is the principle that is involved, more than anything else.

If I may just say a word in connection with the last remark by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, I would say there is no argument but what there are smaller operators in this field than those mentioned earlier by some of my colleagues. However, I think if he had followed those remarks carefully, particularly the last remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West, he would have realized that what was being suggested to the minister was that consideration should be given to a revision of the taxation structure in a manner that would cause taxes to come from the sources from which they should come.
The only thing I should like to say in expressing my agreement with the approach taken by the hon. member for Kootenay West in respect of the resources tax is that I feel, in looking at this proposal, that this parliament is being placed in a horrible position as a result of the stupid action taken by the provincial governments of two of the provinces. It seems to me there can be little argument that this is poor legislation; that it is a bad principle that this parliament should, in effect, be asked to bail out any taxpayers of Canada because certain provincial governments may have introduced certain stupid and illogical methods of collecting taxes in their own fields. While there may be some point in straightening up these anomalies, nevertheless I hope this will be the only precedent for legislation of this kind. We could open the way for other provincial governments to introduce equally ridiculous tax proposals, and then have them come to this parliament to have the taxpayers in those provinces bailed out as well. I hope the minister will make it clear, if approval is given to this proposal, that this parliament is
Income Tax Act
not extending an open invitation to other provincial governments to act in an equally irresponsible manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have very few comments to make on this clause. I appreciate what hon, gentlemen opposite say, on the one hand, that they are in favour of this legislation-with the exception of hon. gentlemen in the corner -and on the other hand, suggest there is something iniquitous about it. I happen to have had the privilege of sitting in on all dominion-provincial conferences since I have been on this side of the house, and in 1957 or 1958, whenever the first one was held. I can tell hon. gentlemen opposite, and hon. gentlemen in the far corner, that this action was not prompted by the tycoons from British Columbia or from Ontario. This action was prompted by requests of the provincial treasurers of those two provinces. These requests were made time and time again, and for that reason we have taken this action.
Personally, I welcome those expanding profit figures which my hon. friend read to me a few minutes ago. They simply bear out what we have always said, that under this government the economy of Canada is expanding and prosperity is greater. I appreciate very much this tribute to our efficient housekeeping indicated by the figures which the hon. member has put before us today. I also remind hon. gentlemen that the larger those figures are the larger the intake of my colleague the Minister of National Revenue which, afterwards, is paid over to me as Minister of Finance. I welcome, therefore, these expanding figures and I hope they grow larger as time goes by.
My hon. friend from Kootenay West said he was talking about a tax philosophy. The reason this action is being taken, Mr. Chairman is, as I said, at the request of the provincial governments and because, as a matter of tax philosophy, we thought it was unfair to this primary industry which was subject to two systems of tax, this income tax, a 41 per cent corporate tax, and then these logging taxes in addition. It is not a matter of double taxation per se, it is the matter of the imposition of this tax upon an industry which provides a great deal of employment. Although there are some large operators, we know there are also some smaller ones, and it is for that reason and on that basis we are amending the act to remit to the taxpayer two thirds of this logging tax, rather than having it deducted from income as heretofore.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to indicate to the hon. member that we are prepared to make a brief statement on the proposition of farm-outs. A common form of farm-out agreement is an agreement under which the holder of gas and oil rights agrees to assign a part of his interest in the production from wells on the property to another person if the other person drills a well or wells to a specified depth, at his own expense, and the drilling is successful. In these circumstances, even though the original holder's rights are made more valuable by reason of the successful drilling, he does not actually receive any payment for the part interest

that he must give up, so there is no amount to be brought into income. Of course, if he later sells the part of the interest which he has retained or any portion of it, the amounts received from the sale must be brought into income.

In fact the history has been that in a great many instances an independent Canadian company has only been able to obtain its entry into the industry via the farm-out route.

Mr. Chairman, I think that we do not look at the development of our natural wealth from the right angle.
Rather, we should ask ourselves: Have we, in this country, the required engineers, miners and machinery for the development of our natural resources? If we do have them, why then go and beg capital in New York, Chicago, Switzerland, Italy, France, Belgium or elsewhere?
We have a wealth of natural resources, we have labour, we have the engineers and we can obtain machinery. Therefore, there is only one thing we do not have: capital.
Clause 23 of the bill bears out my assertion, since its intent is to get foreign corporations to come to this country by granting them tax exemptions. The purpose of clause 23 is not to get engineers, because we have them; it is not to bring in more miners, for we know that we have unemployed miners here in Canada and it is exactly to put them back to work that the government wants to lure foreign corporations to come to this country. Everybody, of course, knows that we have the necessary natural resources. Our problem is that they must be developed with foreign capital.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the Minister of Finance should realize that we have here the essential elements and I mean, mines, natural resources and labour for the operation of our mines. We also have engineers and machinery; therefore, the only thing we

need on top of that is capital. This is a problem he should try to solve and if no solution appears feasible to him I really wonder what problem he could solve?
We do not ask him for miracles. This is not a matter of "growing" mines in the province of Quebec or elsewhere in Canada. The mines are already there. It is not either a question of looking for engineers, we have them. The only thing we ask him is to find means to put capital available for our Canadian companies. The only thing we need is the ticket to develop our natural resources. With reference to this section, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance reminds me of a station master-anywhere in Canada, in Ottawa or Montreal-who would refuse to let people get on the train simply because he forgot to have tickets printed and who would tell the Canadian people: "I cannot sell tickets for I forgot to have them printed, so you cannot get on the train".
What would you think of such a station master? You would say of course that he was remiss in his duty in neglecting to have tickets printed to let those people travel. What would you think of the station master who would let the train pull out without any passenger?
With this section, it is exactly the same situation. The real resources, mines, ores, engineers and machinery are there. The only thing missing is the "ticket" to permit the development of our resources.
Mr. Chairman, one question we might ask the Minister of Finance is this: Which is the most important? The mine itself, the ore it contains, or the capital required to develop the mine? Of course, it is the ore. The mine, the ore, the potential is there. Even with the best intentions in the world, the Minister of Finance absolutely could not create the mine and the ore, but it is his duty to deliver the "ticket" to develop that mine. That, the Minister of Finance must do.
It seems to me that on this discussion of section 23 of Bill No. C-78, it is relatively easy, after the remarks I just made, to understand the Social Credit supporters when they say that what is physically possible should be made financially possible. It is physically possible to develop our mines because we have everything we need. But it is not financially possible, and that is evidenced by the fact that the Minister of Finance will have to get capital from outside the country.
Income Tax Act
But is he not the minister responsible for the Bank of Canada? That being the case, he can use the Bank of Canada to create the money required for the development of our mines and the extraction of the ore that lies there waiting.
People will say that Social Crediters want to manufacture money. No, Mr. Chairman, that is not so. All we want is simply to make financially possible, what according to that section 23, is recognized as being physically possible. We want the Minister of Finance to use that instrument he has, that is, the Bank of Canada, to ensure that the mines of our country will be developed.
Some will raise the cry of inflation. Is capital from Ottawa going to create more inflation than capital from New York? The same amount of money will contribute to the development of our mining industry. What would be the result if the Minister of Finance were to use Canadian instead of foreign capital?
The problem is always the same. By constantly calling upon foreign capital to develop our natural resources, we have reached the point where 70 per cent, or even more, of our industries, our natural resources, our manufactures are developed with foreign capital. All those foreign investments in Canada were made with profit in mind, and each investor gets a profit or an interest from the shares he holds in our country.
That money, I said it yesterday and I am saying it again this afternoon, leaves Canada each year for foreign countries. That is the main reason for the imbalance in our foreign exchange. It is also the reason for the austerity program that has been with us since two or three days after the election of last June 18.
We do not necessarily lay the blame for Canada's present situation on the present Minister of Finance. The finance department was not in his hands when Canada started encouraging foreign investments some 15 or 20 years ago. There have been other ministers of finance and they are the ones who are responsible for the situation in which we find ourselves nowadays because that was the time to prevent foreign investment in our country and they failed to do so. They did exactly the contrary; they encouraged foreign investors to place their capital in Canada. They are the ones who are to blame for Canada's present economic difficulties. The

Income Tax Act
present Minister of Finance cannot therefore be held responsible for the enormous quantity of foreign investments in our country nor for the yearly outflow of Canadian capital under the form of profits and interest.
On the other hand, if the present Minister of Finance continues the ruinous policy of the previous government, if he does not give up that policy which Canada has been following for the past five, ten or 15 years, he will be the one who deserves our criticism. For the time being, however, we blame only the federal ministers of finance of the past 10, 12, 15 or 20 years, whose attitude caused the present situation.
Mr. Chairman, I notice that some of the Liberal members who sit on this side of the house seem to find my remarks funny. It still remains that an economic crisis like the one we are going through right now does not occur overnight.
Mr. Chairman, the present crisis is not, in fact, a true economic crisis, it is just a monetary crisis created by investments of foreign capital in our country. That economic situation was brought about by the Liberal administrations that came before the present government.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to say to the Minister of Finance that if he continues to apply the disastrous policy adopted by his predecessors 15 to 20 years ago, he will be held responsible in his turn, 15 years from now, because then the situation will have become worse.
In fact, if you look at the capital leaving the country at the present time-

You are right, Mr. Chairman, clause 23 deals with the mining of iron ore. I am talking about the mining of iron ore when I say that it proposes to grant an income tax reduction of 15 per cent to nonresident companies that will come and mine iron ore in Canada. That is what I am talking about.

I have no intention of talking in this house about the mining of iron ore because I am not familiar with that matter. However, I know very well that if non-resident corporations, or foreign capitalists, are allowed to develop our Canadian iron ore, then we are certainly creating an economic crisis for the years to come.
Mr. Chairman, if we are dealing with this principle it is because we want to urge the Minister of Finance to cancel section 23 of Bill C-78 now under consideration.
Temporarily, he might perhaps gain an immediate advantage, but such an advantage will always be only immediate.
That provision of the bill will perhaps encourage companies to set up here in this country, since they would benefit from a 15 per cent tax reduction on mining operations. But, Mr. Chairman, if our mines are developed by foreign companies, what will be the result in a few years?
First of all, there will happen what has always happened, that is, that foreign companies will get hold of our ore and will transport it in their countries under that form. And afterwards, it is in those foreign countries that secondary industry will prosper and will transform that ore into secondary or finished products. And what will we have here in Canada? We will simply have given away our natural resources to foreigners; foreign industrialists will have taken over our raw materials to send them to other countries.
Mr. Chairman, the first disadvantage of such a policy is the fact that when foreign companies come here to develop our natural resources, they hasten to transport our raw materials into their own countries, thus promoting there the expansion of secondary industries. It is the progress of secondary industries which brings about increased employment.
The implementation of this section may result in increasing labour demand in other countries, but not in Canada.
The second disadvantage which might result from the implementation of this section is the one to which I referred a moment ago, that is to say, that in eight or ten years from now, when the development of those mines will have begun to progress, the profits made will get out of this country, and it is our monetary system which will still continue to suffer the consequences.
Mr. Chairman, I would ask the Minister of Finance to cancel section 23, not in cancelling income tax for those who develop our ore,

but rather in easing the tax burden for Canadian companies only, and not for foreign companies.
That is why I should like to suggest an amendment to section 23, that is to strike out the words "non-resident corporations", to leave only the words "Canadian corporations only".
Mr. Chairman, if you will kindly give me the time to draw up this amendment, I shall send you a copy of it.

Mr. Chairman, I fully agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Lapointe, and I should like to point out a further aspect of the problem raised by section 23.
In my opinion, this constitutes an economic nonsense and a disturbing inconsistency.
Mention was made yesterday of an additional exemption of $50 for every dependant child, which represents only a crumb for the small wage earners, whereas today it is the intention to exempt foreign companies of 15 per cent of the taxes they had to pay up to now.
That amounts more or less to rejecting the fatted calf, while our Canadian people are not even enjoying a vital minimum.
When will the government realize its sustained inconsistency? Are the heads of foreign corporations in need of an additional purchasing power in order to consume our production? Indeed not, because they will spend that money elsewhere.
Those who are really in need of an increased purchasing power are our people, the low income groups of Canada.
The maintenance of taxes at their present level ensures moreover an ever increasing inflow of foreign capital in our country, which controls over 75 per cent of our economy.
Does the government want at all costs to hand over the control of our economy, and especially of our natural resources, to foreign companies? The government has nothing to gain in reducing the taxes of those companies which, even if they have to pay 15 per cent more to come here and develop our resources, will not hesitate to do so in order to enjoy the enormous advantages they are now getting and which they will never give up, even at the cost of a 15 per cent increase in taxes.
Instead of doing that the government should endeavour to eliminate the causes of the present economic disorder, that is the lack in purchasing power among people who live in such a rich country as ours and do not even have a vital minimum.
Instead of working to reduce foreign corporation taxes, the government should rather

work to increase the tax exemption for dependant children of small wage earners.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would like to say one or two words with respect to this clause, but first I should mention that a few moments ago I was really optimistic with the progress we were making and hoped we would finish the remaining clauses by five o'clock. I would like to speak in an as accomplished a manner and as forcefully as the hon. member for Lapointe has spoken about respect for Canadian industries. I do not think anybody in the house would disagree with the desirability of Canadians owning more and more of Canadian industry. To that policy and to that principle this government subscribes entirely.
It is desirable to increase in every way possible Canadian ownership and Canadian control, but when the 15 per cent tax was imposed in 1960 the principle was recognized at that time that, in some cases due to factors over which we have no control whatsoever, it was necessary to allow certain exemptions from the imposition of that tax, for instance, in the case of banks, insurance companies, corporations whose principal business is transportation or communication, and corporations incorporated before 1867. I think the only one in that last class was the Hudson's Bay Company, and there were also the corporations exempted from tax under section 62.
I am not sure whether the hon. member for Lapointe recognizes that this clause does not prevent the full imposition of income tax on these branches operating in Canada, but that due to certain devices of the tax laws in other countries there are companies which find it inadvisable to incorporate subsidiaries in Canada and therefore they operate through branches. Such branches are taxed completely and entirely on their income to the same extent as any Canadian company and any foreign company incorporated within the country.
What we are doing here is suggesting to the committee that the special 15 per cent tax imposed in 1960 should be lifted from companies engaged, as the clause says, in mining iron ore in Canada because, as I am quite sure the hon. member for Lapointe and other Quebec members know, there are great deposits of iron ore in that province and in other parts of Canada.
It was intended, five or six years ago, when it was thought Canada had a great monopoly of iron ore, that we would go ahead and develop, exploit, manufacture and control the mining of it in this country; but if I may use a rather slang expression, today iron ore

Income Tax Act
is running out of the ears of countries in many parts of the world, such as Venezuela, and certain other countries in Africa and South America. In fact they have richer iron ore and more of it than we have, and were it not for the fact that steel companies had spent millions and millions of dollars developing iron ore companies in Canada I doubt if we would be able to get them to do that at the present time.
It is only very rarely that an individual company can go ahead and meet the great expense of developing a huge iron ore company. To do this you need a consortium of steel companies because you need more than one customer for the iron ore. Without this provision in the bill there is a very great danger some of these investments would not be made and it is for that reason, and that reason alone, that this amendment is being brought forward. It is not anything new or novel. It is an extension of a principle recognized before and made applicable to the mining of iron ore, and these companies are subject to the full taxation laws except for this 15 per cent.

I understand perfectly well what the Minister of Finance has just told us, especially regarding the iron ore in the province of Quebec. It is true that we have lots of minerals in Quebec on the north shore of the St. Lawrence seaway, but when we see the way they are being developed, then that is exactly what we are opposed to. We see our minerals, our raw materials, going out of the province of Quebec at a couple of cents per ton and they come back into the province of Quebec, or Canada, after passing through the United States where they are processed in secondary industries.
We are witnesses to that every day. We see it in Ungava and everywhere else in the province of Quebec. Foreign companies are extracting our minerals at a fast rate, but what do we profit by it? We just have a couple of men working while our minerals are transported to other countries to be processed. It is secondary industry which brings real employment and real wealth to a country, and if Canadian companies were developing our mines and minerals in the province of Quebec, as well as in Canada, we would see secondary industries grow up everywhere.
I recognize that some foreign companies have preferred to invest in Canada, and especially in the province of Quebec; but maybe this is because they have found such conditions here that they can take everything away and bring all the profits to their own countries. That is what we are opposed to in this group. We do not care to see full taxation

imposed on non-resident companies, but we would like to see Canadian companies given much better conditions under which to develop our mines. If a 15 per cent tax is imposed on non-resident companies over what resident companies pay, then surely our resident companies will see they have the benefit of better conditions to develop our mines and natural resources. That is exactly what we are for. The non-resident corporations should have more taxation than the resident corporations. In other words, the resident corporations, the Canadian companies should have better conditions than non-resident corporations to develop our natural resources. Therefore I think my amendment should stand.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador is unavoidably absent today. I feel, therefore, that I should like to say just one word in very warm support of the Minister of Finance. I will tell the committee why very briefly. This summer I was in Labrador City, which happens to be in Newfoundland, and when I commend the minister I would also recommend that he get an atlas, because there is at least as much of this iron ore in Newfoundland as there is in Quebec. I was in Labrador City this summer at a time when one of these iron ore companies was establishing a processing plant for the further processing of the ore here in Canada. We all know that we are on the edge, in this country, of the generation of power from the Hamilton river which is going to make it possible to make steel-certainly it is going to go a long way toward making steel right up in that area of new Quebec and in Labrador-if we have an economic climate that makes it possible to attract the necessary capital to that area.
If we were seeking to give United States companies any advantage over Canadian companies I would just be as much opposed to this as any other hon. member in this house. All we are saying is that the companies that are already there, the companies that were established before 1960 when this tax was put on, should be treated in the same way as companies that have their head offices in Canada. It just happens that the iron companies-the two that are in Newfoundland: one of them is in Quebec as well- though they are in part United States companies have very large Canadian shareholdings of completely Canadian shareholders. Their direction and management to a very great extent, is in the city of Montreal, and to a marked extent in Seven Islands, Labrador City and Wabush City. I do not know of any United States companies that are more conscious of the importance of Canadianizing their operations to the maximum extent possible

than are these companies. I think it is only fair, when they are doing the kind of thing we have all said we wanted them to do, to recognize that fact.
I do know that at the time of confederation 13 years ago there were about 5,000 people in Labrador; and look at the population today. There are going to be 25,000 people at Labrador City and Wabush in the next two or three years. Those people are there with their families, earning a very good living. It is one of the few areas where there has been a real expansion of employment in these last five years, and the expansion of employment has been because there was capital there to provide that employment for Canadians in Canada. I say we should not discriminate and that there is no more reason for not including these companies mining iron ore than there is for not including the other companies.
I think perhaps it would enable us to understand this whole question better if the minister would read the schedule to which "mining iron ore in Canada" is being added, so we would see what companies in 1960 were not subject to this 15 per cent tax, because the 15 per cent tax did not apply to all United States companies. Whether or not the 15 per cent tax was wise is not proper to debate now, but whether or not it was wise, I think it was designed to prevent United States capital coming in and gobbling up Canadian companies that had already developed, rather than to prevent new developments. Perhaps if the minister could tell us what the other categories of companies are that are exempted from that tax, that were exempted in 1960, it would bring the whole matter into rather better perspective.

But I am somewhat confused as the result of the taxation philosophy which he was espousing. Mr. Chairman, it is a pleasure for me to inform the committee, and I think if the Minister of Finance would agree to adopting the same principles as they have in Alberta it would be far better for the government of Canada. The hon. member for Kootenay West should know that in Alberta, when a company comes into that province to develop an oilfield, for example, the government of Alberta keeps one out of every ten barrels of oil they are extracting from

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? Mr. Chairman, according to the actual system, the 15 per cent deduction would help provide more investment and development in our country. We arrive with a proposition. Instead of having foreign capital coming into Canada with which to extract our minerals, we would like to ask the Minister of Finance to use the Bank of Canada to create new capital to invest in our country, so that we will not any longer be responsible to foreign capital but to Canadian capital and we will have our own Canadian investment in the development of our country. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COURT OF CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order concerning the propriety of the introduction of this particular bill by a private member, and I propose to offer for your consideration reasons why this is not a proper bill to be introduced by a private member. Before stating those reasons I should like to congratulate the hon. member on the obvious thoroughness with which he has pursued his objective and the many interesting and, I am sure, useful ideas suggested by him in his bill.
In Beauchesne, fourth edition, page 214, citation 249, it is stated:
No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer.

There are many other citations in Beau-chesne to which I could refer and which have been mentioned by other hon. members when similar occasions have arisen, but I will not refer to them at this moment. In support of this general thesis I should like to quote a few sentences from a recently published book by Professor Dawson entitled "Procedure in the Canadian House of Commons". It is one of the Canadian government series published by the University of Toronto Press. On page 231 there is a section dealing with money bills where Professor Dawson has this to say:
A bill which affects the rights, property or prerogatives of the crown must also be accompanied at some stage in its progress by the consent of the crown. This may be announced at any stage of a bill's passage through the house, although normally before second reading. The minister in charge merely states in the house that the Governor General has been made acquainted with the purpose of the bill and has given his consent for the house to do with it as the house sees fit. A public bill introduced by a private member which affects the prerogatives of the crown must be withdrawn if the crown withholds consent.
I do not think there is any suggestion of consent involved here. The expression of the government's views with respect to this particular matter is clear indeed. During the recent election campaign the Prime Minister announced the intention of the government to introduce such an Indian claims commission. This was followed by a reference to the same matter in the speech from the throne and, as found on page 8 of Votes and Proceedings, a resolution appeared in the name of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration reading as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the establishment of an Indian claims commission and the appointment of its members and staff; to provide for their salaries and expenses; to define the duties of the commission, to authorize it to exercise certain powers and to provide for other related and incidental matters.
Clearly the presence of this resolution preceding the introduction of a bill defines the objective as being one which will make the bill in essence a money bill, and in such cases where there is a resolution the purpose is to determine essentially whether money should be provided for this purpose. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the presence of the resolution in the name of the minister indicates that Bill No. C-19 clearly is a money bill and as such beyond the capacity of a private member to introduce or present to the House of Commons.

Indian Affairs
everything that has been said by the hon. member for Skeena, but I thought it might help Your Honour if I recalled the fact that many times in previous parliaments the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has introduced legislation to vest certain functions in the exchequer court and never before have I heard it suggested, because we suggested that the exchequer court, which is fully paid for, should do new things, that this would constitute a charge. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COURT OF CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that a careful examination of the bill offered by the hon. member for Skeena will definitely disclose that in effect, in pith and substance, it is a money bill. What the hon. member is attempting to do very adroitly is to achieve indirectly something which he is prohibited from doing directly. This is the issue to which he has directed his mind and my submission is that he has failed to achieve this result. I would ask Your Honour to refer to some of the sections of the proposed bill. Section 3 of the bill reads as follows:
The court shall consist of the president, puisne judges and deputy judges of the Exchequer Court of Canada as that court from time to time is constituted;
Then I underline these next words:
2. A deputy judge who is specially appointed for the purposes of this act shall be, notwithstanding anything as to qualifications for appointment in section 8 of the Exchequer Court Act-
Then, the next subsection sets out what the qualifications shall be. I pointed out to Your Honour that under the Exchequer Court Act there are a number of sections which lay down the jurisdiction of the exchequer court. During 1960-61, the then minister of justice introduced a bill amending the Judges Act by which one additional judge was appointed to the exchequer court. At that time it was made plain that the amount of work which was being done by the exchequer court required the appointment of this additional judge. It is quite true that under the

provisions of section 8 of the Exchequer Court Act there is the power to appoint a deputy, but not deputies.
I point out to the hon. member that a careful reading of section 8 of the Exchequer Court Act suggests that there is a limitation to the appointment of a deputy, and that is when one of the judges may be prohibited from carrying on his work. Quite obviously, sir, the hon. member has certain objectives in mind. As the parliamentary secretary has pointed out these laudable objectives deal with a considerable number of cases which will probably arise if legislation such as this is passed. Obviously, if this measure is passed some method of implementing the hon. member's intention will be required; a tribunal of some kind will be required.
My submission is, and I think the hon. member realizes this, that the exchequer court as presently constituted would be totally incapable of devoting the amount of time required to do the work. For this reason, the hon. member has suggested that deputies shall be appointed. This can only presuppose that there will be a charge imposed upon the crown because deputy judges, presently not in existence, will have to be engaged and paid a salary. Of course, the salary of these judges will be a burden upon the crown. This, by itself, is a certain indication that this bill will result in payment being made by the crown.
Then, I refer Your Honour to clause 5 which mentions the fact that the registrar of the Exchequer Court of Canada and the other officers such as clerks, stenographers and so on, shall be the registrar, clerks and stenographers in respect of this proposed court. There is a reference also to travelling expenses. The court proposed by the hon. member is authorized to travel throughout Canada. Quite obviously in doing so the travelling would be on business entirely distinct from the normal jurisdiction of the judges of the exchequer court. The expenses and costs which would be imposed by these services, these travellings, would be additional burdens upon the crown.
I point out to Your Honour that at the moment the exchequer court consists of the president and five puisne judges. According to clause 7, this court of Indian claims which the hon. member proposes to set up will consist of five judges. This would not leave any great number of judges for the ordinary functions of the exchequer court.
Finally, clause 19 makes provision for this court which the hon. member proposes to set up to have the power to request counsel to argue any claim as to any interest that is affected and as to which counsel or an agent does not appear. Then, subclause 4 of clause

19 provides that the court may order the reasonable costs or expenses of preparing a claim to be administrative expenses of the court. Quite obviously, this will result in additional burdens being placed upon the crown. Then, Your Honour, I point out there is a provision that the crown shall be bound by this act. I point out that from time to time, during the course of its deliberations, this court may make decisions which may impose upon the crown the necessity of making certain payments in respect of claims. This, quite obviously, could mean nothing else but a burden on the crown.
In my submission, therefore, I would take it from the mere fact that the hon. member is attempting to engage the services of the exchequer court, and from what he seeks to do, one can come to no other rational conclusion but that there will be additional costs levied upon the crown.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF COURT OF CLAIMS
speechtext:
I wonder if I could be allowed similar latitude, Mr. Speaker, to that which has been allowed the hon. member who has just taken his seat? He did deal with a number of points in connection with the bill which I should like to refute and which are not valid points at all.
He made a reference to clause 3 of the bill which says that the court of Indian claims shall consist, in fact, of the exchequer court. He made a specific reference to part II concerning the appointment of a deputy judge. He set out the qualifications for a deputy judge which differ from those qualifications which are now established for a judge of the exchequer court or a deputy judge of the exchequer court. These qualifications must necessarily be different because the problem with which this court would deal is distinctly different from the problem with which the exchequer court has had to deal. The problem involves long standing grievances of a group within this country who were a nation before coming under European influence and before their rights and freedoms were taken away from them. These qualifications necessarily must be there in order to permit people who are qualified to sit in the international courts of justice, or highly reputed jurists in other countries, to be members of the court. This has nothing to do with the cost involved in the appointment of these deputy judges.
This is covered, and the hon. member for Peace River referred to it, by section 8 of the Exchequer Court Act which says that the governor in council may, for a variety of reasons, appoint a deputy judge to do things for a temporary purpose. This is all this bill seeks to do. Although there is a reference in part I to deputy judges, you will see it means 27507-3-110J
Indian Affairs
the exchequer court including those deputy judges who from time to time constitute it. Whether or not the governor in council wants to set it out in different ways is his business, but the statutory authority is there already. All the bill seeks to do is to take what presently exists as a court in this land, and a court incidentally which will have experience in such matters as land valuation and taxation, and give it specific authority; that is all it does. The measure would give to that court specific authority to deal with the particular claims of the Indian people on the basis of that Latin phrase ex aequo et bono, which you will understand more readily than I.
This court would deal with the long standing complaints of these native people in the most equitable manner possible. I do not believe that is possible under the rules of court procedure and evidence as they stand at the present time. This is the design, purely and simply behind this bill, and it is not to do indirectly what I cannot do directly nor is it to spend money of the crown. The design is to use this court which already exists within the structure of the law of this country, to give it special authority and to give to the native Indian people of these provinces a square deal in respect of the complaints which have been built up for over many, many years.
I submit that all of these other references to expenses, to judges' salaries, even to the question of authorizing expenses in clause 19(4), to which the hon. member for Peace River made reference, even to the extent of paying the charges, the court costs and legal fees incurred by natives in processing their claims, do not constitute a new charge on the crown but are already covered by virtue of the statutory authority now existing in the Exchequer Court itself.
On the question of whether or not there is a prohibition against the introduction or the moving of second reading, I submit to Your Honour that I myself, on two or three occasions in other parliaments, introduced a bill to bind the crown to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act so that civil servants in this country would have the same rights as other people. No objection was taken to that bill; in fact, cabinet ministers and parliamentary secretaries engaged in the debates upon it. The principle involved in that bill was to bring equality to a group of people employed in the public service of Canada by binding those people to the act, which is precisely similar to what I seek to do here.
In essence, Mr. Speaker, I submit that all of the arguments that have been presented so far by those objecting to this bill, all of

Indian Affairs
the arguments revolving around the expenditure of money, are not valid arguments. I could go further in dealing with the various clauses referred to by the hon. member for Peace River but I shall content myself by submitting that all authority for expenses and payments of money is covered in statutory form by the Exchequer Court Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought I was addressing my remarks to the Chair. At least I was looking in your direction. I shall try to be as brief as possible because I am sure other hon. members will wish to speak. Native Indians are in a very peculiar situation in this country. They are involved in the understanding that we have about relationships between nations as distinct from a group of citizens within a country, because when the so-called white man-and I use the expression "so-called" because I do not like the term "white man"-came to this country, and in the years following the discovery of the American continent, this nation was populated by Indian people and the resources of the nation were exploited by them. They had jurisdiction and authority and control and were, in fact, a group of nations to themselves with some of them not having knowledge of others in other parts of the country.
The fact that they came to be called Indians was the result of a mistake made by Christopher Columbus, and this is why our British Columbia natives on the Pacific coast today prefer to be called Haidas because they do not see why they should perpetuate the

mistake Columbus made. Recent anthropological studies in the area near Vancouver and in other parts of the B.C. mainland have shown they had settlements dating back
4,000	or 5,000 years.
Their whole concept of ownership of land, their social structure and their economic life were entirely different from that understood by people of European extraction such as the English, French, Spanish and the like. When these two concepts came into conflict with each other a great deal of confusion and misunderstanding developed, especially among the native Indian people. As a result of that, over the years there have developed grievances over, primarily, the land question, grievances over the wording of the treaties, treaties which were written, designed and worded by people who spoke English and explained them to the native Indian people, who did not speak English and could not write. Any examination of those treaties will show, I am sure, that the Indian people were misled and in fact cheated by the treaties that were signed many years ago.
In British Columbia we have a situation in which there are no treaties except one which was signed with the Hudson's Bay Company in 1850, I think it was, involving some 350 square miles of land, and an area of 134,000 acres in the Peace river country covered by treaty No. 8, which primarily covers the northern part of Alberta. We in British Columbia have a problem different from that which concerns natives in other parts of Canada, in that there is the claim in British Columbia that the native Indian population still has the aboriginal title to that province, that it was never extinguished, that it was never purchased from them, there was no treaty signed, no agreement, no war or wars in which they were a defeated nation or group of people. All that happened was that the crown moved in and took over the area without any compensation or any extinguishment of that aboriginal title. I would ask the house to remember that when the native Indian people think of title to land, they do not think of it as we do, in terms of deeds, pieces of paper and measured lots; they think of it in terms of their hereditary concept of title and communal ownership of the land and its resources.
This bill is designed to establish a court in which these claims, disputes and long standing grievances can be dealt with. The joint Senate and House of Commons committee which reported to this parliament last year recommended the establishment of an Indian claims commission to deal with a number of things. It specifically mentioned the British Columbia land question and the
Indian Affairs
Oka land dispute. The principle, as I mentioned earlier, is that the court should look at these claims on the basic principle of fairness and equitability and that the provisions of the Canada Evidence Act, with all its strictures and rules, should not apply. I say that because it is impossible, with many of these claims, to use rules of evidence to prove a particular case of ownership. The ownership, for the sake of argument, over a trap line is one of inheritance from fathers and mothers from time immemorial. It is impossible, in many cases, to actually prove that such ownership rests in the hands of one individual. The principle is that the court would look at these things and consider evidence which they think fair, reasonable and decent, and then act upon those particular grounds.
We also want to make sure that, because these native people have been so unfairly and unjustly treated over the years, the burden of expense does not fall upon them to process their cases before this particular court. This, again, was a unanimous recommendation of the joint Senate and House of Commons committee, that there is a responsibility for legal costs, and fees for processing and arguing their claims should be borne out of the cost structure of the exchequer court or the court itself. The purpose, I suppose, would be primarily to keep this matter before the government and before the public, to help bring public pressure to bear upon the government to take the initiative in presenting legislation of its own.
There is a notice on the order paper, to which reference has already been made. I hope that notice is proceeded with at the earliest possible moment and the commission as envisaged by the government is established. I do not have any great doubts about what will happen to this particular bill, regardless of your ruling, Mr. Speaker. If you get around to ruling in its favour, I am quite sure that in the one hour at one's disposal every few days it will never come to a vote.
I know there are legal minds in this parliament-we listened to one of them earlier today -who will try to dissect this bill in all possible ways to show why it is inoperative, and so on. To me that is a minor concern. The main principle is to deal with the long standing grievances that have rancoured the native Indian people in this country for many, many years and finally bring to them the solutions which we promised hundreds of years ago.

OFFICE OF THE PRIME MINISTER Province of Quebec
September 19, 1962.
The Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, P.C., Q.C., Prime Minister of Canada Ottawa, Canada
My dear Prime Minister,
In reply to your letter of August 27 with regard to the proposed amendment of section 94A of the British North America Act, I must inform you that the provincial legislature has just been dissolved.
My government feels that only the legislature is empowered to deal with such a matter.
In the circumstances, it seems proper that I should wait until the new legislature is convened before pursuing this matter any further.
I wish to make it clear that this does not imply in the least that I am thinking of revising the position set forth in my previous letters.
Yours very truly,
Jean Lesage.
Ottawa, August 27, 1962
Honourable Jean Lesage, P.C., LL.D. Premier of the province of Quebec Parliament Buildings Quebec, P.Q.
My dear Premier:
I refer to the correspondence we exchanged last January and February concerning a proposed amendment to section 94A of the British North America Act, which would authorize parliament to legislate not only in relation to old age pensions, as is the case now, but also in relation to pensions and other benefits incidental to, or conducive to the better operation and administration of, a scheme of old age pensions.
More specifically, the proposed amendment would authorize parliament not only to pass a law creating a contributory and progressive
old age pension plan but would also make it possible to include provisions regarding the payment of benefits, in some cases, to widows and children, as well as to contributors who become disabled before reaching the pensionable age. You replied to my letter on January 24; I wrote to you again on February 3 and you replied again on February 8.
Similar letters were addressed to the premiers of all the other nine provinces on January 17. Eight of them replied without delay, saying that they agreed to the proposed amendment. I hope to hear shortly from the only premier (Newfoundland) who has not replied yet. The explanation of the scope of the amendment we contemplate, as it was given in my letter of January 17, was found sufficient by the eight premiers who have expressed their agreement.
I hope that I have sufficiently indicated the objectives of the proposed amendment so that you and your colleagues will find it possible to advise us of your agreement.
According to the information I have, it was not customary in the past, when the provinces were invited to agree to amendments to the British North America Act, to supply them with the details of the provisions that the government and parliament hoped to adopt under their legislative powers. In 1941 and in 1951 in particular, when the federal government proposed some constitutional amendments, I am told that the consultations between the federal and provincial governments did not result in any effort on the part of any party either to furnish or request detailed information on the legislative measures that were to follow the adoption of the constitutional amendments.
In any case, I am convinced that you are not without realizing that, even if we were to furnish details of the legislation we contemplate, it would not prevent subsequent amendments to the law in the light of policy changes.
I am confident that you will agree with me that it is in the public interest, at the federal as well as the provincial levels, that parliament be invested with specific jurisdiction

to legislate in the way proposed in the amendment submitted to your consideration.
I earnestly hope that you are now prepared to agree to the proposal I have already submitted to you.
Your sincerely,
John G. Diefenbaker

Ottawa,
August 25th, 1962
My dear Premier,
I wrote you on January 17th, 1962, setting forth the terms of a proposed amendment of section 94A of the British North America Act to authorize parliament to make laws not only in relation to old age pensions, as it is now authorized to do, but also pensions and other benefits incidental and conducive to better operation and administration of a scheme of old age pensions. I requested the concurrence of Newfoundland in the proposed amendment of the British North America Act.
I wrote to the premiers of all the provinces at the same time. I have received responses from all of them with the exception of yourself. Eight of nine immediately concurred in the proposal.
A decision on this subject is now urgently required. I should be obliged, therefore, for an expression of your government's views. May I express the hope that Newfoundland will concur in the proposed amendment?
Yours sincerely,
John G. Diefenbaker. The Honourable J. R. Smallwood, M.H.A., Premier of Newfoundland,
St. John's, Newfoundland.
OFFICE OF THE PREMIER Province of British Columbia
February 12th, 1962
Right Honourable John G. Diefenbaker, Q.C., Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Canada.
My dear Prime Minister:
I acknowledge and thank you for your letter of January 17th, describing your plans for improving the Canadian social security system by authorizing contributory old age pensions for those not presently covered, but who can reasonably afford additional provision for their old age and certain ancillary benefits.
In view of the fact that present pension and annuity issuing authority is so broadly based, it is not clear to my advisors why a constitutional change should be necessary to implement the measures you describe.
However, there is no objection to the proposed amendment to section 94A of the British North America Act in the form proposed.
Yours truly,
W. A. C. Bennett, Premier.

Prime Minister of Canada,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ontario.
My dear Prime Minister,
In compliance with the request you made in your letter of February 3, I re-examined the text of the amendment you propose to bring to section 94A of the British North America Act.
Having done so, I am even more convinced that it would have been impossible for me to bring such a proposition before the legislative assembly without being able to explain its scope adequately by means of a detailed description of the legislation to be put forward through that amendment.
I should point out that the proposed text is extremely vague and indefinite. It seems to me that the phrase "benefits incidental and conducive to a better operation and administration of a scheme of old age pensions" could be made to cover a great number of things which, at the present time, all come under provincial jurisdiction.
Obviously, the question does not involve the subordinate provisions to which any jurisdiction usually extends according to well-established principles of interpretation. Surely, what is sought is an extension beyond that limit, and nowhere do I see the dividing line which would be chosen.
I find it impossible to concede that the provincial jurisdiction is adequately safeguarded by the reservation concerning laws passed by a provincial legislative assembly. When the federal parliament becomes entitled to legislate in matters under provincial legislative authority, the jurisdiction of the provinces is necessarily reduced even if they are left with some legislative power. Indeed, from then on, such power can only be exercised subordinately.

For those reasons, once again, I must say I find it impossible to bring before the legislative assembly a proposed constitutional amendment without having on hand a detailed description of your proposal.
I intend to table a copy of this letter in the legislative assembly next Tuesday.
Yours sincerely, (signed) Jean Lesage

Toronto, Ontario.
February 6, 1962. Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
I learn with much pleasure of your proposals to develop a contributory social security scheme for the aged which will also include and extend to the disabled and survivors (including children) of contributors who have died.
It is our considered opinion that the only proper way to add strength to our social security planning for the future lies in the establishment of a contributory scheme enabling contributors to establish their right to receive benefits on a prescribed basis in keeping with their previous contributions.
May I say, therefore, that the government of Ontario would concur in and facilitate proper and reasonable plans by your government resulting in a contributory social insurance program becoming a reality.
Yours very truly, John P. Robarts.
The Right Honourable John G. Diefenbaker,

THE PREMIER Fredericton
February 5th, 1962 Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
I regret the delay in replying to your letter of January 17th which was received during my absence.
The improvement of the Canadian social security system through the inclusion of a plan for graduated old age pensions on a contributory basis in addition to the basic old age security pension will be well received in all quarters.
The government of New Brunswick is pleased to concur in the amendment of section 94A of the British North America Act in the form proposed in your letter and will support the submission of such an amendment to the parliament at Westminster.
Yours sincerely,
Louis J. Robichaud. The Right Honourable John Diefenbaker, Prime Minister of Canada Ottawa, Ontario.
